For most candidates, that meant performance analysis. For me, it meant every instinct would have an audience. And for Elira, standing beside me with a hidden Black Circle protection around her throat, it meant someone had already noticed where to press.

I let the false Green Circle at my wrist settle into the harmless rhythm I had practiced for years: weak enough to be dismissed, stable enough to avoid pity, ordinary enough to survive inspection.

The problem was that ordinary had become difficult to maintain around people I wanted to protect.

I looked through the corridor windows toward the bright campus outside, where students were already turning selection notices into celebration, rivalry, and ambition.

To them, the world had become larger. To me, it had become narrower.

Every road now seemed to lead through an arena, an archive, or a room where someone like Professor Halden would ask the right question in the wrong way.

For the first time since the rumors began, they stopped feeling harmless.

Because affection was no longer only gossip. Someone had started measuring it.

---

Two days after the initial qualification notices, the real selection process began.

Aurelis Arcane Academy felt less like a school and more like a kingdom preparing for war while pretending it was education.

Training grounds filled before sunrise. Strategy rooms stayed occupied between classes. Students who had not qualified watched those who had with mixtures of admiration, resentment, relief, and private calculation. Every corridor carried the same tension: who would represent Aurelis, who would fail, and who would embarrass themselves before the visiting academies arrived.

The rumors about Elira and me hadn't vanished, either, though they had shifted from scandal into background weather. By the time we walked into the central strategy hall, Aira had stopped cataloging new theories and settled for glaring at anyone who slowed down near our shoulders.

The room was broader than a normal classroom, circular and tiered, with floating screens displaying tournament categories, prior Aurelis performance rankings, and projected team structures. Faculty lined the outer wall with clipboards, crystal tablets, and expressions ranging from professional interest to ruthless evaluation.

Professor Halden stood at the center.

So did Instructor Dren, along with two senior examiners: Lady Seraphine Morn of tactical studies, a severe Red Circle strategist with unnervingly precise diction, and Master Ilyas Thorn, a veteran Blue Circle combat instructor whose face looked carved from endurance and disappointment.

Professor Halden raised one hand, and the low conversation faded.

Professor Halden: "Today begins the internal selection phase. Not all of you will remain in contention. Some will be sorted into support categories. Some into alternate reserves. A select few will make up Aurelis's main team."

A display opened behind him.

**SELECTION PHASE - DAY ONE**  
**INDIVIDUAL EVALUATION**  
**TEAM POTENTIAL MAPPING**  
**ADAPTIVE COMPATIBILITY SCORING**

Professor Halden: "Your first evaluations will not be public duels."

That disappointed several students immediately. Professor Halden noticed and did not care.

Professor Halden: "This tournament is won by whole schools, not vanity. We are not selecting the loudest students. We are selecting the most effective."

At the edge of the room, Leon stood a little straighter at that, perhaps trying to signal that he, too, now valued effectiveness over spectacle. I doubted the transformation was complete.

Lady Seraphine stepped forward.

Lady Seraphine: "You will be tested in three stages today. First, sharp mana control. Second, quick thinking when the field shifts. Third, trial teamwork. Every score matters."

Aira leaned slightly toward me.

Aira: "I dislike every phrase she just used."

Haru: "You dislike competence when it's pointed at you."

Aira: "That is a hostile interpretation of my personality."

Elira, on my other side, lowered her voice just enough for only us to hear.

Elira: "It's also accurate."

Aira gave her a wounded look.

Aira: "You're supposed to be kind."

Elira: "I am. That was very gentle."

The first evaluation took place in the **Lattice Chamber**, a long, white training hall divided by suspended crystal nodes. Each student stood on a marked platform while mana-sensitive targets floated through shifting patterns around them. The objective was not power, but exactness.

A student had to strike, redirect, shield, or stabilize the targets according to rapidly changing instructions projected above the chamber.

Too much force cost points.
Too slow a reaction cost points.
The wrong spell choice cost points.

This was the kind of test that embarrassed prodigies who relied on rank alone.

One by one, students were called.

A Red Circle spear specialist overcommitted and shattered a target meant to be preserved.
A Blue Circle earth user reacted too slowly to an inversion sequence.
A Green Circle support caster performed unexpectedly well by compensating for lower output with flawless timing.

The examiners noted everything.

When Aira's turn came, she walked to the platform like someone walking into an unfair office trap.

Aira: "If this goes badly, I want both of you to remember me kindly."

Haru: "That feels dramatic."

Aira: "That's because I'm under pressure."

Elira: "You'll do well."

Aira glanced at her.

Aira: "If you say encouraging things in that voice, it becomes very difficult to fail with dignity."

She stepped onto the platform.

Then, to the surprise of several nearby students, she became completely different.

The uncertainty vanished. The complaints vanished. The humor thinned into focus.

Blue mana gathered around her hands in crisp, efficient lines. Her specialty was fast defense and support: shaping small currents of water and air, weaving layered shields, turning spells aside, and adapting on the fly.

The projection flashed.

**INTERCEPT**

Three targets shot forward at staggered angles.

Aira moved immediately. A thin ribbon of water mana snapped from her hand, nudging the first target off course without damaging it. A compressed air pulse slowed the second. A rotating micro-barrier caught the third and lowered it gently into the stabilizing field.

**CONTAIN**

She sealed a destabilized crystal in a transparent water shell without cracking it.

**REVERSE**

She redirected an incoming force wave back through a rotating prism array and stopped it dead before it touched the platform edge.

By the end of the sequence, the chamber was quiet.

Aira exhaled and stepped off the platform with visible relief.

Master Thorn looked down at his score slate.

Master Thorn: "Sharp support reflexes. Steady nerve under stacked orders. Clean mana use."

Aira blinked.

Aira: "That was suspiciously close to praise."

Lady Seraphine: "Do not become dependent on it."

Aira: "There it is."

She returned to us with the deeply offended dignity of someone who had done very well against her preference.

Haru: "You were strong."

Aira: "I understand. It's upsetting."

Elira smiled.

Elira: "You're wasted on false modesty."

Aira: "That wasn't modesty. It was despair management."

Elira's turn came not long after.

No one pretended not to watch.

The chamber itself seemed to sharpen around her the moment she stepped onto the platform. Her Yellow Circle crest glowed at her collarbone, while the dark necklace resting quietly below it looked like ordinary stone, its true design known only to us.

The projection flashed rapidly.

**INTERCEPT**  
**SPLIT**  
**STABILIZE**  
**REINFORCE**  
**NULL OVERFLOW**

Elira tried to hold all five instructions as one thought.

Gold-white light divided cleanly across the first four targets. She redirected two, split a third, and built a shield cage around the unsteady crystal before it finished dropping. Too early. The crystal shifted beat.

Her beautiful web became the wrong shape around it.

The overflow struck one rigid corner and rebounded through the platform. A target crystal jumped its rail. Elira cut three finished spells at once to catch it before it hit the floor. The crystal survived.

The stabilization ring did not.

Red failure light crossed one section of the platform.

Elira stood inside the remains of her own spellwork, breathing hard and looking personally betrayed by her own guesswork.

Master Thorn: "Continue."

Elira exhaled once and cast again.

This time she waited for the node to answer before deciding what it meant. Her next web was less graceful and more accurate. The remaining targets settled without colliding, though one balance light stayed yellow instead of green.

Silence held for one beat. Then the applause came anyway, smaller and more honest.

Professor Halden's score notation moved.

Lady Seraphine: "Exceptional recovery."

Master Thorn: "High control. One early guess. One spell left out of tune."

Elira stepped down with her jaw tight.

Aira: "You saved the crystal."

Elira: "I trapped the overflow before it existed."

Haru: "You guessed the standard frequency."

Her gold eyes cut toward me. For one second I thought I had made it worse. Then she exhaled.

Elira: "Yes. I was solving the instruction I expected."

Aira: "I would offer comfort, but you look like you intend to duel the very idea of guessing early."

Elira: "It knows what it did."

Then it was my turn.

The chamber grew quieter in a different way: expectation, curiosity, and a little suspicion.

The Green Circle transfer had already disrupted one hierarchy and dismantled Leon in public. Now everyone wanted to know whether that had been context, luck, or something stranger.

I stepped onto the platform.

My false Green Circle crest stayed steady at my wrist beneath my cuff. My real power remained buried.

The projection flashed.

**INTERCEPT**

Simple enough.

I used the minimum output required, redirecting the first target with steady bracing and a sharp angle rather than force.

**CONTAIN**

A weak-looking shield formed around the crystal. Deliberately weak-looking. It held perfectly.

**NULL OVERFLOW**

A destabilized node descended too quickly for most Greens to manage cleanly. I compressed the mana field around it just enough to stop the surge without revealing how precise the compression truly was.

The sequence escalated.

**SPLIT**  
**REVERSE**  
**REINFORCE**

I kept the work good enough to be undeniable and ordinary enough to survive inspection.

Then something moved behind the instructions. Not mana. Metal.

One of the upper guide anchors had cracked where old stress hid beneath fresh polish. A suspended silver weight shifted above the junior Green assistant resetting targets at the platform edge.

The evaluation system did not mark it. The weight was equipment, not threat.

I saw the fracture before it made sound. That was the problem.

If I moved now, Halden would know I had perceived what the instruments had not. If I waited until the crack became visible, the assistant might not move fast enough.

The Black Circle offered a thousand quiet corrections. I chose one.

A thread narrower than the false Green crest at my wrist should have been able to form passed through the guide rail. I did not stop the weight. I changed its fall by the width of two fingers. The anchor snapped.

Silver struck the platform beside the assistant instead of his shoulder.

He stumbled backward. My active shield collapsed because I had taken attention from it. The contained crystal rolled free and stopped against the safety rim.

Every evaluation light went red. No one applauded. Good.

Master Thorn crossed the barrier first.

Master Thorn: "Injury?"

The assistant looked at the fallen weight, then at his own hands.

Assistant: "No."

Lady Seraphine: "That anchor was outside the active sequence."

Haru: "It was falling."

Assistant: "I did not see it until it moved."

Neither had the instruments.

Professor Halden crouched beside the broken metal. He ran one finger along the old fracture and then looked at the silver weight. Its impact mark sat two fingers away from the path gravity should have given it. He looked at me.

Professor Halden: "Mr. Aerlen, what did you cast?"

The easy lie arrived first. Reflex. Luck. A Green bracing thread catching the rail after the crack.

Elira stood beyond the barrier with the expression of someone who had just failed because she acted before evidence and knew exactly what my silence was trying to do.

Haru: "A correction thread."

Professor Halden: "Before or after the anchor broke?"

I could feel every student listening.

Haru: "Before I heard it break."

Halden's face became very still.

Master Thorn checked the assistant's shoulder and then the shattered shield.

Master Thorn: "Safety save accepted. Active hold test failed. Control score stays high. Completion score cut."

The junior assistant found his voice.

Assistant: "Cut? He stopped that from hitting me."

Master Thorn looked at him.

Assistant: "Sorry. I know I am not scoring."

Master Thorn: "You are correct anyway. Equipment failure is entered separately. Mr. Aerlen's choice still broke the assigned condition. Both facts remain."

The answer did not make me hero or failure. I distrusted it less for that.

Lady Seraphine studied the faint green crest at my wrist.

Lady Seraphine: "Your mana stretch still doesn't match the small reserve on your wrist."

Haru: "I focus on control."

Professor Halden rose with the broken anchor in his hand.

Professor Halden: "Clearly."

His tone gave away nothing. Which made it worse.

I stepped off the platform.

Aira: "That was less subtle than you think."

Haru: "Someone was under it."

Aira's expression lost its humor.

Aira: "I know."

Elira looked at me quietly.

Elira: "You chose before the room gave you permission."

Haru: "Yes."

Elira glanced back at the reset platform lamps, remembering her own yellow warning light.

Elira: "So did I."

The difference between our choices stood on the platform rubbing an uninjured shoulder. Neither of us pretended that erased the question Halden had begun asking.

---

The second stage was worse, not because it was combat-heavy, but because it was psychological.

The **Adaptive Responsiveness Hall** was a shifting arena of illusion walls, half-shields, warped terrain, and surprise training beasts. Students were sent in alone and forced to react to unstable conditions with limited information.

Fog. Darkness. False allies. Delayed spell response. Enemy decoys. Mana interference. Changing terrain.

In other words: panic, professionally organized.

Aira's description, not mine. She said it while staring at the entrance gate before her turn.

Aira: "This is panic, professionally organized."

Haru: "That's a strong summary."

Aira: "If I don't come back, use my notes respectfully."

Elira: "You'll come back."

Aira: "Yes, but perhaps changed."

She did, in fact, come back: sweaty, irritated, and carrying one of the better times of the rotation.

Aira: "I dislike being competent in stressful environments. It rewards the wrong parts of my personality."

Elira went in next and emerged with the fastest completion time recorded so far. No one was surprised.

The truly notable result came from a Red Circle heir named **Cassian Veyr**, whose fire power was among the strongest in the room, though his patience was close to zero. He blasted through the course in spectacular fashion, earning both admiration and criticism.

That mattered. This tournament would need symbols, yes, but not unstable ones.

My own run was uneventful externally and irritating internally.

The illusion beasts were too easy to read. The decoys felt hollow in their mana. The traps followed patterns I could spot at a glance.

I completed the course with a high score, careful not to break the evaluation by being faster than people would accept from a Green.

That still placed me near the top, which did not improve my anonymity.

By the time the afternoon phase ended, students were exhausted, overstimulated, and fully aware that Aurelis intended to build a tournament team capable not just of competing, but dominating. Examiners ushered the remaining candidates back across to the circular **strategy chamber** for the closing posting before dismissal.

The final exercise of the day appeared once everyone had filed inside.

**Provisional Team Integration Mapping**

That got everyone's attention back immediately.

Names began to appear in groups on the suspended projection: temporary squads, mixed-rank combinations, different affinities, balance testing.

Aira squinted at the screen.

Aira: "Please let this be reasonable."

It wasn't. Our names appeared together.

**TEAM CANDIDATE GROUP THREE**  
**ELIRA VALE**  
**AIRA SOLEN**  
**CASSIAN VEYR**  
**HARU AERLEN**  
**LEON VAREK**

Aira stared at the projection in numb disbelief.

Aira: "No."

Elira read it once, then again.

Elira: "That is... aggressive."

Haru: "Strategically or emotionally?"

Aira turned to me.

Aira: "Yes."

Across the chamber, Leon had also seen the assignment. His expression froze for a second before flattening into something controlled and difficult.

---

## Interlude: Leon - Reclassification

Leon Varek did not admit he was wrong about people. He adjusted. That was different.

Wrong implied carelessness. Leon was not careless. He made fast assessments, corrected for new data, and moved forward before anyone could turn the correction into confession.

Haru Aerlen had become inconvenient data. Green Circle. Transfer. Quiet. Too calm in the arena. Too controlled when Leon pushed.

His visible crest said he lacked the output to challenge properly, yet every instinct Leon had left after losing in public refused to dismiss him. Haru was neither naive enough to need unsolicited protection nor arrogant enough to hate cleanly.

The categories did not hold. Leon disliked that more than the loss.

Loss had grammar. You trained harder. You found the gap. You corrected the weakness before someone else used it again.

Haru did not feel like a gap. He felt like a door Leon had kicked and then discovered was not locked, only waiting to see whether he would try the handle.

Elira Vale stood beside him by choice.

That made the assignment worse. Not because Leon wanted her attention; he had told himself that twice and believed it enough to stop examining the sentence. Because Elira did not make careless choices, and if she had chosen to stand near Haru after seeing more than Leon had seen, then Leon's old categories were not merely incomplete. They were embarrassing.

The team list glowed above the chamber. Elira. Aira. Cassian. Haru. Leon.

His name at the end looked like punishment until he noticed Haru's name was not first. That bothered him. It should not have.

Leon looked at the quiet Green Circle transfer and made the smallest correction he could tolerate. Neither rival nor target. Teammate, provisionally.

The provision mattered. So did the choice.

---

Cassian Veyr, by contrast, just laughed.

Tall, red-haired, and carrying the kind of confidence usually produced by old family power and excellent combat results, Cassian stepped toward our side of the hall with open amusement.

Cassian: "Well. This looks volatile."

Aira: "You say that like it's positive."

Cassian looked at her and grinned.

Cassian: "I enjoy difficult combinations."

Aira: "That is exactly the kind of sentence a problem says."

Leon approached a moment later, slower and far less pleased.

Leon: "If we are being evaluated as a team, I assume everyone understands that personal theatrics will not be tolerated."

Aira blinked at him.

Aira: "You truly said that out loud."

Cassian laughed again. Elira's tone remained polite.

Elira: "Then we should all avoid them."

Leon looked as if he was trying to decide whether that had been agreement or criticism. It had been both.

Professor Halden's voice carried across the room.

Professor Halden: "Group Three. Remain after dismissal. Your first joint exercise begins immediately."

Aira closed her eyes.

Aira: "It does."

I looked at the team list once more.

A Yellow Circle prodigy.
A calm Blue support specialist.
A volatile Red combat heir.
A humiliated Blue rival.
And me.

This was not a team; it was an experiment. Either Aurelis believed this combination had exceptional potential, or Professor Halden wanted to see what happened when pressure was applied to all the fault lines at once.

Given the way his gaze found me again from across the chamber, I suspected both.

The other candidate groups filtered out of the strategy chamber in clusters of relief, annoyance, or self-important discussion, leaving only the five of us and the senior evaluators behind.

The room felt larger once it emptied. More exposed.

Professor Halden stood at the center with his hands clasped behind his back. Instructor Dren remained near the projection array, unreadable as ever. Lady Seraphine and Master Thorn took positions at opposite ends of the chamber, clearly preparing to observe rather than assist.

In other words, if this went badly, it was supposed to.

Professor Halden: "Group Three was assembled to test high-variance compatibility."

Aira folded her arms.

Aira: "A dignified way of saying you expect problems."

Professor Halden looked at her over the edge of his lenses.

Professor Halden: "Miss Solen, if I expected only problems, I would not waste faculty time observing you."

Aira paused.

Aira: "That was almost encouraging. I resent that."

Cassian let out a short laugh.

Cassian: "I like her."

Aira: "That makes one of us."

Leon clicked his tongue softly.

Leon: "Can we begin without turning this into a social exercise?"

Haru: "You say that as if group function isn't partly social."

Leon's eyes flicked to me at once.

Leon: "Some of us are here to compete seriously."

Cassian glanced between us with open interest.

Cassian: "Did I miss a duel history?"

Aira: "Several, spiritually."

Elira exhaled very quietly beside me. Not quite a laugh. Close.

Professor Halden raised one hand, and a three-dimensional model of the academy grounds appeared above the floor.

Professor Halden: "Tactical extraction. Enter, secure the simulated relic core, adapt, return it to the recovery zone."

The model shifted. A forested terrain bloomed into view, divided by ravines, false ruins, and layered barrier pockets.

Professor Halden: "The field will change while you are inside."

Aira: "Because static rules might let us keep our dignity."

Lady Seraphine stepped forward.

Lady Seraphine: "Success is not enough. Following orders, clear calls, sharing the load, handling clashes. If you win while functioning like a catastrophe, your score will reflect it."

Cassian smiled.

Cassian: "That seems targeted."

Lady Seraphine: "If you feel targeted, improve."

He looked delighted by that.

Master Thorn gestured toward the west doors.

Master Thorn: "Simulation arena. Move."

---

The simulation field occupied an enormous lower training sector beneath the western grounds. It was one of the academy's most expensive strategic facilities: a shifting battleground run by terrain runes, layered illusions, weather wards, and free-roaming stone beasts.

When the doors opened, we stepped into what looked like the edge of an artificial wilderness.

Dense trees.
Broken stone ruins.
A shallow stream running through a rocky cut.
Mist hanging low over uneven ground.

At the center of the field, several crystal pylons hummed softly, feeding power into the simulation grid. Above them, a timer ignited in red light.

**TEAM EXERCISE BEGINS IN 00:30**

Aira looked at the terrain and then at the sky, as if silently asking why existence was like this.

Aira: "I would like everyone to know I prefer maps when they're not actively trying to humiliate me."

Cassian rolled one shoulder, already loosening into combat readiness.

Cassian: "Forest, ruins, limited visibility. Could be worse."

Aira stared at him.

Aira: "You are definitely someone who says 'could be worse' moments before it becomes worse."

Elira stepped forward just enough to draw the group's focus without forcing it.

Elira: "We have thirty seconds. We need initial roles."

Leon answered immediately.

Leon: "Fine. Cassian and I take forward pressure. Elira supports central control. Solen handles barrier analysis and rear adaptation. Haru..."

He paused a fraction too long.

Leon: "Haru can assist where needed."

Aira looked offended on my behalf before I had time to decide whether I cared.

Cassian glanced at me.

Cassian: "You're assigning the unknown variable to 'assist where needed'?"

Leon: "I'm assigning based on demonstrated output."

Haru: "That's one interpretation."

Elira's voice remained even.

Elira: "No. We assign based on actual behavior under pressure."

Leon turned to her.

Leon: "And what does that suggest?"

Elira: "That Haru reads patterns faster than most people here."

There was no hesitation in the way she said it. None.

I felt Leon notice that as much as the words themselves.

Elira continued.

Elira: "Cassian applies force well. Aira stabilizes and redirects. You're strongest when your casting has structure and support. I can hold the center steady."

She looked at me.

Elira: "Haru reads the ground and calls the hidden shifts before they happen."

Cassian's eyebrows rose.

Cassian: "You trust him that much?"

Elira: "Yes."

Immediate. Uncomplicated.

That word did not do good things to my ability to remain emotionally detached.

Leon heard it too. His expression tightened very slightly.

Aira, however, looked mostly vindicated.

Aira: "Good. Finally a role assignment based on reality."

The timer hit ten seconds.

Professor Halden's voice echoed through the field.

Professor Halden: "Begin."

---

We moved.

Cassian took the lead naturally, flames gathering in sharp coils around his fists without fully manifesting. Leon stayed just off his right flank, water mana already threading in low currents around the ground to test for hidden traps. Aira remained central, scanning the barrier lines and ambient shifts. Elira walked with the calm of someone whose presence alone stabilized the team's rhythm.

I watched the mana beneath the terrain instead of the trees and ruins. Simulation environments always had logic; even chaos was built on design.

The stream to our left was too quiet.
The mist on the right was denser than the ambient temperature justified.
The old stone path ahead rippled faintly, hiding delayed trap runes.

Haru: "Left stream is a trap. Don't cross it directly. Right mist probably hides fake targets. Path ahead has pressure runes under the third and sixth stones."

Cassian looked back mid-stride.

Cassian: "You see all that this quickly?"

Haru: "Enough of it."

Leon did not look at me.

Leon: "Or he's guessing confidently."

Aira: "That would matter more if he kept being wrong."

Cassian laughed.

Cassian: "All right, Green. Lead with your eyes, then."

We adjusted course. Aira used a low-pressure water film to reveal hidden lines in the ground. The third and sixth stones lit up instantly, trap confirmed. Leon said nothing.

That silence was almost more satisfying than rebuttal.

We cut through a side corridor of broken ruins instead, where the first constructs attacked.

They emerged from the stone like armored beasts made of packed mana and bronze light, four-legged and fast, jaws opening with sharpened arcane edges.

Cassian grinned.

Cassian: "Finally."

He launched forward in a burst of red-orange fire, striking the first construct with a hardened elbow that shattered its shoulder plate. Leon swept the second one's legs out with slicing water crescents. Efficient. Controlled. Better than during our direct matches. Competition suited him better than wounded pride.

The second wave came from above.

Haru: "Upper left."

Elira was already moving.

Golden light rose in a curved shield just as two airborne constructs dropped from the ruins. They hit the barrier and rebounded into open range. Aira trapped one in a compressed water sphere long enough for Cassian to destroy it with a downward arc of flame, while Leon's rising water blade sliced the second clean out of the air.

Then a fifth construct-heavy-armored and creeping along the ruined wall blind spot-dropped straight toward Aira's back.

Leon reacted a beat too late. I didn't.

I stepped in, knocked its lunge aside with a tight burst of force, and drove it into the stone wall hard enough to crack its core.

Cassian whistled.

Cassian: "You really aren't a normal Green, are you?"

Haru: "I get that a lot."

Aira: "Not enough, honestly."

We kept moving.

The deeper we went into the simulation, the more obvious the evaluators' intention became. This was no simple retrieval exercise; it was a pressure chamber.

Every five minutes the terrain changed.
The stream rose and became electrically charged.
The ruins shifted positions.
False objective signatures appeared in the distance to split decision-making.
At one point, illusion duplicates of our own team members appeared through the trees, each calling conflicting instructions.

Aira was the first to identify the pattern.

Aira: "The false voices are too clean. Real voices always drag a little mana static at the edges in fog this heavy."

Haru: "Agreed. Ignore anything that sounds easier than the situation deserves."

Cassian smiled.

Cassian: "That may be your best tactical principle yet."

Then the first real problem arrived.

The objective chamber, a ruined circular structure at the center of the field, was protected by a layered shield lock that needed four matching streams of magic poured into four anchor stones at once.

We reached the outer ring and stopped.

Aira immediately knelt to inspect the runes.

Aira: "This is not one lock. It's four linked locks sharing the same kickback."

Leon crouched opposite her, running water mana across the etched lines.

Leon: "If one anchor is forced incorrectly, the others reset."

Cassian folded his arms.

Cassian: "Can we break it?"

Aira and Leon answered together.

Aira: "No."

Leon: "No."

Cassian looked mildly offended.

Elira stepped toward the ring.

Elira: "What does it require?"

Aira traced the nearest sigil.

Aira: "Balanced input, not brute force. Four stones. Different jobs. One has to shape the flow, one has to steady it, one has to push it, and one has to soak up the kickback."

Cassian pointed at himself.

Cassian: "The push stone. Obviously."

Leon nodded toward the fluid channels.

Leon: "I can handle shaping."

Aira: "I'll steady it."

Elira looked at the final node.

Elira: "Then I'll soak the kickback."

I looked more closely at the line structure and felt the problem immediately.

Haru: "No."

Everyone turned toward me.

Elira: "Why?"

I stepped nearer the lock.

Haru: "Because the kickback stone isn't just a shield. It shifts to match whoever touches it, and it blows up any wobble from the other three."

Aira's eyes widened as she re-read the rune pattern.

Aira: "He's right."

Leon frowned.

Leon: "Then who takes it?"

The answer was obvious. I looked at the node.

Haru: "I will."

Leon's disbelief was immediate.

Leon: "Absolutely not."

Cassian looked intrigued.

Cassian: "Why not? If he can handle it, let him."

Leon: "Because if he fails, the whole structure resets."

Aira straightened.

Aira: "And if Elira takes it, her bright magic might overload that mirror effect. Haru is the steadiest pick if the stone cares about control more than raw power."

Leon looked between the three of us like betrayal had turned into school policy.

Leon: "We are seriously trusting the Green on the key node?"

Elira's gaze held steady.

Elira: "Yes."

That word again, delivered without a flicker of doubt.

Cassian's grin sharpened.

Cassian: "Well, now I want to see it."

We took positions: Aira at the steadying stone, Leon at shaping, Cassian at the push stone, and me at the kickback anchor. Elira stood central, ready to field-correct if the chamber destabilized.

Aira counted us in.

Aira: "On three. One. Two. Three."

Mana flowed.

Cassian fed sharp, measured force into his node. The rune blazed red-orange. Leon's water mana coiled into the second, smoothing the spinning rhythm. Aira wove fine support lines into the third, holding the lock's structure together.

Then I touched the fourth.

Even suppressed, the Black Circle made control like this easy. Too easy.

The shifting stone drank in my mana and lost its glow. Neither overloaded nor erratic, simply still.

It had recognized something beyond the scope of its own design and, finding no way to meaningfully reflect it, settled for obedience.

The risk sat cold under my ribs. I carefully reduced the flow, forcing the structure to behave as though it were merely impressed by excellent Green Circle control.

The lock rotated. The four anchors aligned. The barrier split open.

Cassian laughed aloud.

Cassian: "That was absurdly clean."

Aira looked at me with narrowed eyes.

Aira: "You make too many impossible things look tidy."

Leon said nothing, watching me now with a more serious kind of attention.

Inside the chamber, the relic core floated above a pedestal of broken stone, a crystal orb filled with swirling blue-white energy. Simulated, of course, but valuable to the scoring system all the same.

Elira stepped toward it.

Elira: "We secure and return."

Professor Halden's voice rang through the arena.

Professor Halden: "Complication phase."

The chamber floor dropped.

An illusion, though backed with enough real force to make your stomach drop.

The circular ruin shattered into floating platforms. The forest beyond darkened into stormlight. The relic core split into three copies, each giving off different magic traces.

Cassian laughed again.

Cassian: "There it is."

Aira: "Why do you always sound pleased when things become unreasonable?"

Cassian: "Because that's when people become interesting."

Leon pointed immediately.

Leon: "Center core. Strongest output. That's the real one."

Haru: "No."

Elira turned to me.

Elira: "Which?"

I studied the three orbs.
One burned too brightly, obvious bait.
One was too stable for a field under active disruption.
The third, slightly dimmer and off to the left, was imperfect in exactly the way reality usually was.

Haru: "Left."

Leon: "Based on what?"

Haru: "The others look too clean for a broken field. The left orb carries the same rough static as the floating platforms."

Aira looked once and immediately nodded.

Aira: "He's right again."

Cassian grinned at Leon.

Cassian: "You're losing a difficult argument, Blue."

Leon ignored him, but only barely.

The constructs returned then, stronger than before, winged and humanoid this time, armed with projected weapons and shield arrays. Three descended toward the left platform. Two cut off our retreat.

Elira moved first.

Golden light spread outward in a radiant ring that slowed the nearest attackers and stabilized the collapsing edge of the platform. Aira braced the underside of the stone with tight water-spun webs. Leon cut down one construct with a focused crescent blade that was honestly impressive.

Cassian leapt straight through the middle of the chaos, fire erupting around him in controlled bursts as he smashed one of the shielded constructs apart.

I moved to the relic core.

The moment my hand closed around it, the entire simulation screamed.

Red light flooded the arena.

**OBJECTIVE SECURED**  
**EXTRACTION WINDOW: 02:00**

A two-minute retreat under escalating pressure. Naturally.

Leon and Cassian hammered a gap straight through the two stunned constructs blocking the exit while Elira's radiant arc swept the last broken flyer clear of the edge.

Haru: "Move."

Everyone moved at once. This time no one questioned who had called it.

That, more than anything else, told me the team exercise was changing us. Not into friends, certainly not yet, but into something more useful: people beginning to trust competence despite themselves.

We ran the extraction path with the relic core protected at center. Aira adjusted routes on the fly. Leon finally stopped resisting team logic and focused on what he did well: fluid control, barrier cutting, path shaping. Cassian broke anything too slow to avoid. Elira held the group together like a sun at the center of moving gravity.

And I watched the shifting field, calling the invisible changes before they happened.

Then the simulation became personal.

The forest ahead split open into a narrow ravine crossed by a broken bridge, and a student appeared on the far side. Not a real student: a lifelike construct wearing the uniform of an Aurelis first-year, kneeling with one hand pressed to a cracked barrier while shadow beasts hammered against it from three directions. The construct was built well enough to breathe unevenly, to tremble, and to look up with panic that did not belong to a training field.

The relic core pulsed in my hands.

The recovery route glowed beyond the ravine. The timer continued falling.

Leon: "It's a decoy."

Aira: "It is also a scoring condition. Look at the barrier line."

She was right. A thin silver marker glowed under the construct's feet, nearly hidden by dust.

**OPTIONAL RESCUE NODE**

Cassian's fire flared around one wrist.

Cassian: "We can clear that."

Leon: "And lose time."

Cassian: "Then we lose time."

Leon turned sharply.

Leon: "We are carrying the objective."

Elira looked at the construct, then at the route, then at us. Her expression did not change, but the air around her warmed by one degree.

Elira: "If this were real, we would not leave them."

Leon: "It is not real."

Haru: "The evaluators are watching whether that matters."

That stopped him.

For a heartbeat, Leon looked exactly like someone standing between the person he had been and the teammate he was not yet sure he could become.

Aira's voice softened without losing its edge.

Aira: "If we rescue wrong, we fail both objectives. If we ignore it, we tell the faculty what kind of victory we are willing to accept."

The timer hit forty-seven seconds.

No time for a speech. Good. Speeches were often what people used when action frightened them.

Haru: "Cassian, break the beasts from the outside only. Do not touch the construct's barrier. Leon, bridge the gap with hardened water over Aira's support line. Elira, shield the relic core from the shockwave. Aira, call collapse timing."

For once, no one argued.

Cassian moved first, crossing the broken bridge with three explosive steps and striking the nearest shadow beast so cleanly it shattered without throwing debris into the construct. Leon threw a water line under the bridge and hardened it into a temporary path. Aira layered fine support lines over his work, teeth clenched in concentration, before the two of them dashed across to anchor the far landing.

Elira stepped beside me, gold light closing around the relic core.

Elira: "You included yourself nowhere."

Haru: "I am holding the problem."

Elira: "You are part of the team."

The sentence landed faster than I expected.

Haru: "Then I am holding the center."

Her eyes softened for half a second.

Then the ravine wall cracked.

Aira: "Collapse in five."

Leon: "Cassian!"

Cassian caught the false student by the back of the uniform and hurled them away from the edge onto solid stone beside the recovery path, where Leon and Aira caught the construct together in a water-cushioned barrier. Elira sealed the shockwave backlash and darted onto the bridge just ahead of me.

I sprinted across the cracked bridge right behind her, keeping the shielded relic core tight against my chest.

The ravine tried to eat the path under me.

For one dangerous instant, the Black Circle offered the simplest solution: erase the collapse, rewrite the bridge, make the simulation remember a safer world.

I did none of those things.

I used one Green-level burst of force at the exact right joint and let the broken bridge survive long enough to be crossed by people who had earned the rescue themselves.

We reached the far side as the ravine folded shut behind us.

The construct dissolved into silver light.

**RESCUE NODE CLEARED**

Leon stared at the fading marker, breathing hard.

Leon: "That cost us twelve seconds."

Aira: "It also added rescue credit."

Cassian rolled his shoulders, expression sharper now.

Cassian: "Worth it."

Leon looked as if he wanted to disagree. Then he looked at Elira, at Aira, and at the path we had not abandoned.

Leon: "Next time, call the bridge sooner."

That was not an apology. It was more useful than one.

Three hidden mines beneath the southern ledge.
A collapsing bridge illusion masking a safe path to the right.
A delayed trap spell hidden inside the fake exit gate.

I caught the first two.

I almost missed the third because Elira's shield flickered at the edge of my vision and my attention went to her before the field.

Leon saw my eyes shift.

Leon: "Exit gate, right seam."

I cut the warning short with a nod and adjusted the route.

We adapted, again and again.

We crossed into the recovery zone with seventeen seconds remaining, and the entire observation gallery fell silent.

We had won not because we were the strongest squad in the room, but because we had refused to choose between victory and each other.

Beyond the fading walls of the simulation waited a tournament designed to make that refusal costly.

---

## Coda: Cassian Counts Exits

Cassian Veyr hated standing still after a fight, so he climbed up to the empty observation gallery while the cleaning sigils were still sweeping arena dust into neat silver rows.

He rolled his left shoulder until the joint popped, shook a stray spark off his knuckles, and leaned his forearms over the stone rail. From up here, the simulation field looked smaller and less dramatic, more like a box built to test how much weight a handful of teenagers could take before someone cracked.

Out of old Red-house habit, he counted exits anyway. Six clean doors. Two maintenance grates. One high ventilation arch that technically counted as an escape route if you had enough fire-step momentum and zero respect for your own ankles.

Haru had spotted every dead corner down there before Cassian had even finished lighting his hands. That should have made Cassian relax. Instead, it left an itch behind his ribs.

Down in the corridor below, voices faded toward the washrooms. Leon was finally dropping the bruised-pride act because looking foolish had stopped feeling safer than doing the work. Aira still talked like every evaluation was a personal insult, right up until the second she had to catch three people's mistakes at once. Elira watched Haru the way someone watched a friend standing too close to a cliff edge, steady and ready to grab his collar if he stepped back.

And Haru kept reaching for the smallest spell in the room when Cassian would have bet his family's signet ring there was more behind it.

Cassian flicked the last ember off his thumb and pushed away from the rail.

If the tournament wanted to break Group Three, it could get in line. Cassian planned to stay close enough to catch the moment the quiet Green ran out of small answers.

===== EPISODE 4 =====

# Episode 4: **The Shape of a Team**

The recovery zone flared white beneath our feet.

The relic core in my hands dissolved into particles of blue light, marking a clean extraction. Around the edge of the simulation field, the crystal pylons dimmed one by one. The storm-dark sky above the arena peeled away into clear runic glass. Trees, ruins, mist, and broken terrain all shimmered and collapsed back into raw, orderly mana.

Reality returned in layers, and with it came silence: the weight of being scored, watched, and judged.

The faculty had seen everything. So had the assistant judges taking notes from the outer ring, and the recording crystals set high above the empty observation gallery.

Aurelis had wanted to test whether our group would fracture. Instead, we had succeeded: messily at times, unevenly, reluctantly, and undeniably.

Cassian rolled his shoulders and let out a satisfied breath.

Cassian: "Well. That was fun."

Aira bent over with both hands on her knees.

Aira: "Your definition of fun requires review."

Leon wiped sweat from his jaw and exhaled slowly, trying very hard to look as though nothing about the exercise had surprised him.

Elira stood straight, composed as ever, though the flush in her cheeks and the slight rise and fall of her breathing made the effort she'd spent visible to anyone paying attention.

I was paying attention. That had become a problem of its own.

Master Thorn stepped forward first, glancing at the timing crystal.

Master Thorn: "Fast recovery. Faster adjustment than expected."

Lady Seraphine looked over her notes.

Lady Seraphine: "Communication tightened after the halfway mark. Early rank friction hurt you. By the end, practical sense beat pride."

Her gaze shifted, very briefly, toward Leon and Cassian. Appropriate.

Cassian grinned openly.

Cassian: "Almost complimentary."

Lady Seraphine: "Do not get used to that either."

Cassian looked delighted, which I suspected was not the intended effect.

Professor Halden approached the edge of the field with his hands clasped behind his back.

Professor Halden: "Interesting."

That was all he said at first. Somehow, from him, it sounded less like praise and more like a blade being tested for sharpness.

His eyes moved across the team: pausing on Elira with expected approval, on Aira with increased interest, on Cassian with cautious doubt, and on Leon with cool disappointment.

Then on me.

Professor Halden: "Mr. Aerlen."

Haru: "Professor."

Professor Halden: "Your eye for patterns keeps outrunning your visible profile."

There were many possible answers to that, most of them bad.

Haru: "The team made the timing work."

Professor Halden's expression did not change.

Professor Halden: "Clearly."

He turned away before the exchange could deepen, which was almost worse than if he had pressed.

Aira leaned just slightly toward me.

Aira: "I'm beginning to dislike the way he says simple words."

Haru: "That seems healthy."

Elira glanced at me briefly, just long enough for the warning inside it to land. Be careful.

I knew. The problem was that caution became harder every time someone smart watched too closely.

---

The official score projections were posted by evening.

Aurelis did not believe in suspense when it could create more useful forms of stress.

Students crowded around the central announcement wall in the main academic court, reading the updated rankings with the focus of people trying not to visibly panic.

Large floating panels displayed category scores, team-fit ratings, and early picks for tournament roles.

Aira stood beside me with her arms crossed and the expression of someone preparing to disagree with existence.

Aira: "If I've somehow become a top support candidate, I'm going to need time to resent my own competence."

Haru: "That seems manageable."

Aira: "For you, perhaps."

The panel shifted. Our group's data appeared.

**GROUP THREE - PROVISIONAL TEAM METRIC**  
**Extraction Success: High**  
**Adaptation Rating: Exceptional**  
**Conflict Stabilization: Moderate to High**  
**Strategic Versatility: Outstanding**

Below that, individual performance notes began to scroll.

**Elira Vale - Principal Candidate: Multi-Category Core Representative**  
**Cassian Veyr - Principal Candidate: Heavy Combat / Breaker Role**  
**Aira Solen - Principal Candidate: Tactical Support / Control Systems**  
**Leon Varek - Secondary Principal Candidate: Midline Control / Fluid Modulation**  
**Haru Aerlen - Principal Candidate: Adaptive Field Reading / Duel Reserve / Tactical Flex**

Aira read the last line twice, then again.

Aira: "They gave you three roles."

Haru: "That seems inefficient."

Aira turned to stare at me.

Aira: "No, Haru, it sounds alarming."

Students around us had started noticing too. Blue Circle candidates a few steps away exchanged glances. One Red Circle fourth-year let out a short laugh of disbelief.

Student: "A Green got principal status?"

And just like that, the tension around my existence at Aurelis sharpened again. It was one thing to be odd; it was another to have the academy back it in writing.

Elira arrived through the crowd a moment later, moving with her usual calm gravity. She looked at the panel once, then at me.

Elira: "You expected this?"

Haru: "No."

Aira: "I did. Unfortunately."

Elira's mouth curved slightly.

Elira: "Then congratulations seem appropriate."

Aira pointed between us.

Aira: "Don't say it like that. He'll accept it too calmly."

Haru: "Thank you."

Aira closed her eyes.

Aira: "There. Exactly."

From across the court, Cassian Veyr raised a hand in easy greeting when he saw us. The movement drew no small amount of attention. He made his way through the other candidates without seeming to care which social rules he was stepping on.

Cassian: "Well, that settles it."

Aira: "What does it settle?"

Cassian stopped beside us and glanced at the panel.

Cassian: "That we're the most interesting team candidate by far."

Aira: "That is not the reassuring phrase you think it is."

Cassian grinned.

Cassian: "You're the support specialist, Solen. You exist to reassure."

Aira: "I exist to survive the school's decisions."

Cassian's attention shifted to me.

Cassian: "You're causing a social crisis, Green."

Haru: "Apparently."

Cassian: "Do you enjoy that?"

Haru: "Not particularly."

Cassian looked almost disappointed.

Cassian: "That's a shame. You're very good at it."

Elira, beside me, seemed faintly amused.

Elira: "That may be because he never tries."

Cassian laughed once.

Cassian: "That makes it worse. Excellent."

Before the conversation could become stranger, another presence entered the edge of the crowd. Leon.

The murmurs around the announcement wall shifted at once, not because people feared him, but because they were waiting to see whether he would react badly.

To his credit, he did not. At least not publicly.

He stopped near the panel, read the rankings, and looked at his own line with a controlled expression. Secondary Principal Candidate was still a strong spot, especially after how badly he'd lost face lately.

Then his gaze moved to mine. Measured. Careful.

Leon: "So they really are building around utility."

Cassian glanced at him.

Cassian: "Is that your polite version of surprise?"

Leon ignored him.

Leon: "I admit, Aerlen, I expected the faculty to be less eager to reward something that looks this strange on paper."

Aira stared.

Aira: "That may be the most elegant insult I've heard all week."

Haru: "I'm learning to appreciate creativity."

Leon's eyes narrowed a fraction, though the reaction was smaller than it would have been before. Good. He was adapting. Which meant he might eventually become useful, or more dangerous. Often those were the same thing.

Leon looked at the team metrics again.

Leon: "If Group Three remains together, we will need better coordination than what we had in the simulation."

Cassian: "That sounded almost like teamwork."

Leon: "Take a moment to recover from the shock."

Cassian laughed. Aira blinked.

Aira: "Are we improving or becoming more sarcastic?"

Haru: "Both."

Elira: "That can still be improvement."

For a brief second, all five of us stood there under the floating rankings, surrounded by staring students and fresh rumor energy, and I could almost see the shape of the thing Aurelis was trying to build.

Neither harmony nor friendship. Capability.

A team made of unstable parts that might, under enough pressure, become stronger than neater pairings. A dangerous theory, but not an impossible one.

The theory became harder to ignore when we were ordered into a closed debrief instead of released to dinner.

The room assigned to us was one of the smaller strategy classrooms beneath the east wing, all black glass tables, wall-mounted maps, and chairs designed by someone who believed comfort weakened discipline. A crystal recorder floated above the center table, its light glowing a steady blue.

Aira sat down and immediately pointed at it.

Aira: "I want that thing to know I am participating under protest."

The recorder pulsed once, dutifully.

Cassian dropped into the chair opposite her.

Cassian: "It likes you."

Aira: "That is the tragedy of my life."

Leon remained standing for a moment, eyes on the replay slate already forming above the table. The simulation had been rendered into clean blue lines: our route, our mistakes, our corrections, the rescue node, the final extraction.

There was no cheering or rumor. Just proof.

Elira took the seat beside me. She did not reach for my hand here; too many crystals, too many possible logs. But her knee touched mine lightly under the table, a quiet point of contact no recorder would understand.

Lady Seraphine's voice entered through the recorder.

Lady Seraphine: "Group Three will review three failures and three strengths. Start without our help. We will judge the discussion afterward."

The light dimmed.

Aira stared at the crystal.

Aira: "They are making us evaluate ourselves."

Leon: "That is standard."

Aira: "No. Standard is an instructor telling us we were disappointing in specific ways. This requires emotional effort."

Cassian leaned forward, suddenly more serious.

Cassian: "First failure. I wanted to break the barrier lock."

Aira blinked.

Aira: "That was... direct."

Cassian: "I am capable of learning when insulted by architecture."

Leon: "You also nearly overcommitted on the rescue node."

Cassian's smile sharpened.

Cassian: "Nearly."

Leon: "Nearly still matters."

For one heartbeat, the old version of Leon showed through: proud, exacting, ready to turn a correction into a rank contest.

Then he looked at the replay of himself insisting the false student was only a decoy. His expression tightened.

Leon: "Second failure. I cared more about the goal than the choice behind it."

The room went quieter. No one made a joke.

That was how I knew the sentence had cost him something.

Cassian leaned back, firelight low at his wrist.

Cassian: "We can't save everyone in a real fight."

He said it lightly. Too lightly: the kind of lightness people used when a sentence had already cut them once and they had decided jokes were cheaper than bleeding in public.

Elira noticed. So did Aira. For once, even Leon did not correct him immediately.

Cassian's thumb moved across the old signet ring on his hand. Red Circle heir jewelry was usually decorative arrogance. His looked worn at the edge, as if someone had turned it too often while waiting for news that arrived too late.

Cassian: "My family calls it triage. Very noble word. Makes leaving someone behind sound like strategy instead of memory."

The fire at his wrist shrank to a thin ember.

Cassian: "I am not fond of that kind of strategy."

Elira answered with the same calm she used in combat.

Elira: "Then we practice saving everyone now, so we know how when it matters. A tournament will try to make us choose between winning and remaining ourselves. We need to decide before the field decides for us."

Aira looked at her.

Aira: "That works as a team principle."

Cassian tapped the table once.

Cassian: "Fine. Principle one: we do not abandon people for cleaner victories."

Leon did not look away from the replay.

Leon: "Agreed."

Aira's eyes softened, but her voice stayed dry.

Aira: "I hate that we are becoming admirable. It raises expectations."

Then the replay shifted to my route calls.

The room became uncomfortable in a different way. Blue lines traced every warning I had called out before anyone could see proof: trap, decoy, collapse, anchor, false core, real core, safe path. Too many correct answers. Too little visible reason.

Leon watched the sequence twice.

Leon: "Third failure."

I looked at him. He looked back.

Leon: "We still do not know how to use Haru without exposing him to every question in the room."

That was not the accusation I expected. It was more dangerous because it was useful.

Aira sat back slowly.

Aira: "That is... annoyingly insightful."

Leon: "Try not to sound shocked."

Cassian grinned.

Cassian: "No, let her have this. I was shocked."

Elira's gaze remained on me.

Elira: "Then principle two: we build explanations before people demand them."

Haru: "You are all assuming this remains our group."

Aira pointed at the replay slate.

Aira: "Haru. Look at that mess and tell me the faculty won't get attached to it."

I looked. Five colored paths crossed, split, collided, corrected, and finally converged into the recovery zone with seventeen seconds remaining. It was not elegant. It was alive.

Haru: "They will become attached."

Cassian leaned back, satisfied.

Cassian: "Good. Then principle three: if anyone asks, all our success came from overwhelming charm."

Leon: "Rejected."

Aira: "Violently rejected."

Elira smiled faintly.

Haru: "Recorded."

The crystal above the table pulsed again. Somewhere, Lady Seraphine was probably writing something severe.

For the first time, I found I did not mind.

---

The next morning confirmed it.

Group Three had been summoned for private advanced training.

That alone was enough to draw attention. Private training slots were usually saved for confirmed team leads or students the faculty wanted to watch up close. In my case, the second possibility felt unpleasantly likely.

We met at dawn in the upper combat terrace where the eastern towers cast long shadows over the practice rings. The air was cool, the campus quieter than usual. Most students were not yet awake enough to be ambitious.

Professor Halden was already there. So were Instructor Dren and Lady Seraphine.

Aira took one look at the faculty lineup and sighed.

Aira: "I'm beginning to suspect we're not a training group. We're a research incident."

Professor Halden heard her.

Professor Halden: "If that were true, Miss Solen, I would not have informed you."

Aira: "That is not actually comforting."

Cassian stretched his arms over his head.

Cassian: "Can we start? Standing still this early feels unnatural."

Lady Seraphine gestured toward the marked rings.

Lady Seraphine: "Today's focus is role compression."

Leon frowned.

Leon: "Role compression?"

Instructor Dren answered.

Instructor Dren: "You all did well when everyone got to stay in their best role. That's useful. It's also fragile. In a tournament, people get cut off. Plans break. If one person gets knocked out of place, the whole team can fall apart."

Professor Halden stepped forward.

Professor Halden: "We want to see if this team still works when you lose what you're comfortable with."

Aira: "That is a remarkably hostile way to describe education."

Instructor Dren: "Yes."

He dropped one palm onto the terrace seal, and the practice rings lit pale blue beneath our boots. That ended the discussion.

The drill was simple in concept and terrible in execution. Every ten minutes, one team member would be removed from their preferred function: Cassian pulled off the front line, Aira knocked out of her steady support spot, Leon stripped of his water control over the ground, Elira barred from anchoring the center, and me cut off from calling moves early.

The exercise was built to make each of us uncomfortable in different ways.

The first round removed Cassian from direct engagement and forced him to guard the back line and cover gaps. He hated it immediately.

Cassian: "This is insulting."

Aira: "No, this is growth."

Cassian: "I preferred you when you were complaining."

His first interception proved the point against him. Cassian moved too aggressively toward a flank construct, shattered it beautifully, and left the rear lane open for a second attack to slip through.

Aira caught the breach with a barrier that made a sound like offended glass.

Aira: "Growth usually includes not abandoning the thing you are protecting."

Still, he adapted faster than expected. For all his love of impact, he had sharp instinct for incoming threats and proved surprisingly good at breaking attacks before they reached the center.

The second round pulled Aira out of her support spot and put her in charge of calling movement.

Aira: "This is malicious."

Elira: "You can do it."

Aira: "Your faith is oppressive."

She did it anyway, and very well.

The third round took Leon out of his careful setup and forced him to fight on instinct. That one exposed the most.

Leon was strong, refined, and skilled, but much of his confidence depended on control and steady timing. Without them, he became less certain and less efficient. He froze for half a breath when the second construct changed angle without warning, frustration flashing across his face because he had no clean setup to work from.

Aira: "Half-step left, then cut on my count."

He moved on her timing. It worked. He noticed that too, and to his credit, instead of lashing out, he adjusted.

By the fourth rotation, when Elira was barred from acting as central commander, the drill became truly interesting.

Without meaning to, the rest of us had already started orbiting around her. Pulling her out left an instant hole.

Cassian wanted motion.
Leon wanted structure.
Aira wanted coherence.

They all looked at me. I did not enjoy that.

Aira: "Well?"

Haru: "Why are you asking me?"

Aira: "Because you already mapped the next three exchanges in your head."

Cassian grinned.

Cassian: "She's got you there."

Leon looked irritated that the assessment was accurate.

Leon: "If you have a plan, say it."

I looked at the incoming construct pattern: three heavy attack lanes, one fake center, and a late strike from the side.

Haru: "I'm not replacing her. I'm holding her position until she's back. Cassian left lane, but don't commit past the second marker. Leon cuts the false center and forces the real flank reveal. Aira, hold mid-height and feed him angles. Elira, stay back on the right-don't step in unless the outer ring breaks."

They moved.

It failed on the second exchange.

The false center broke early. Leon turned to force the flank reveal exactly as I had told him. That left Aira's upper lane open half a breath sooner than my pattern allowed.

Cassian saw the construct diving toward her. He crossed the second marker.

Haru: "Cassian, hold..."

He did not.

His Red Circle struck the diving construct apart. The blast saved Aira's lane and exposed his own. A delayed spear came through the left gap, hit the reserve ring beside Elira, and shattered the stone score post behind her.

Instructor Dren dropped the entire field. Silence landed with the dust.

Elira had not been hit. Aira's sleeve was scorched where Cassian's fire passed too close. Leon stood in the dead center with his blade raised against a flank that no longer existed.

The score crystal displayed one word.

**FAILED.**

I looked at Cassian first.

Haru: "You left the lane."

His grin had vanished.

Cassian: "The construct had Aira."

Haru: "She had the middle height."

Aira held up the burned edge of her sleeve.

Aira: "I did until the center opened early."

Leon: "Your correction came late."

Haru: "You followed the false center after it changed."

Leon: "Because you told me to force the flank reveal."

The answer struck harder than the accusation. They had followed me. That was not the same as trusting me.

I had given each person a path and mistaken obedience for coordination. When the construct changed, Leon protected the instruction, Cassian protected Aira, and I protected the plan until the field broke around it.

Elira stepped out of the reserve ring.

Elira: "Haru."

I knew what she was going to say and still wanted her not to.

Elira: "You planned for our strengths. You did not plan for us to disagree with you."

Haru: "There was no time."

Elira: "There was enough time to give six commands."

Cassian looked toward the shattered post. His hands were open now, fire gone.

Cassian: "I should have called the break before I crossed."

Aira: "I should have called that I lost elevation."

Leon lowered his blade.

Leon: "I should have stopped following a dead instruction."

No one offered me a matching sentence. They waited.

Haru: "I should have told you what mattered instead of deciding every movement."

Professor Halden's pen moved. I hated the sound.

Instructor Dren reset the field with one palm against the central seal. The shattered score post stayed shattered.

Instructor Dren: "Again. No central commander. Call out what you see, what you're doing, and what you can't hold. Anyone giving step-by-step orders loses the right to speak."

Aira stared at him.

Aira: "You can lose the right to talk in a fight?"

Instructor Dren: "You are closest to finding out."

The constructs rose.

This time I did not map three exchanges aloud.

Haru: "False center. Left delay."

Cassian: "Taking left until second marker. If Aira drops, I cross."

Aira: "Mid-height unstable. I can hold one break, not two."

Leon: "I force center after her call."

Elira stayed inside the reserve ring.

Elira: "Right ring can absorb one spear. I choose which."

The wave entered. Nothing looked elegant.

Cassian let the first flank construct pass farther than he liked. Aira redirected it instead of waiting for him to destroy it. Leon saw the false center open and held position, jaw tight, until Aira shouted.

Aira: "Now."

He cut.

The real flank emerged high. I called the angle, not the answer.

Haru: "Right, descending."

Elira chose not to absorb it.

For one frightening beat, I thought she had missed.

Then the spear crossed her empty reserve ring and entered Cassian's lane where he had already turned to meet it. His fire broke its point. Leon caught the remaining shaft with an ugly Blue barrier that knocked him to one knee.

The left lane opened again. Cassian could have taken the final construct and secured the clean finish. He looked at Leon instead.

Cassian: "Can you hold?"

Leon: "No."

Cassian abandoned the point and caught the failing barrier with heat beneath it. Aira took the last construct alone. Her water line missed the center, clipped one edge, and sent the target tumbling across the recovery boundary instead of landing upright.

The field went dark. The score crystal considered us.

**FUNCTIONAL. INCOMPLETE.**

Leon remained on one knee. Cassian offered a hand. Leon looked at it, irritated by needing it, then took it.

Lady Seraphine: "One target missed. Formation held. Nobody left behind."

Instructor Dren pointed at the broken post.

Instructor Dren: "Cost visible. Better."

Professor Halden looked at me.

Professor Halden: "Seeing ahead is useful. Assuming you're right is not the same thing. Learn the difference."

I wanted to argue that I had never been certain. The shattered stone behind Elira made that excuse not worth saying aloud.

Haru: "Understood."

As we reset, Elira stepped near enough that no one else needed to hear.

Elira: "You trusted us to follow."

Haru: "Yes."

Elira: "Next time, trust us to contradict you."

Across the ring, Aira inspected her scorched sleeve.

Aira: "I would like the record to show that growth is expensive and this uniform was new."

Cassian: "I saved the person inside it."

Aira: "You also burned the person inside it."

Leon rolled his aching shoulder.

Leon: "Both facts remain."

No one called us flawless. We were still summoned back for the next training hour.

---

Later that afternoon, the second major tournament notice arrived. This one was public.

Posted in every central corridor, projected over the courtyard, and delivered to candidate groups through official crystal dispatch:

**INTER-NATIONAL SCHOOLS TOURNAMENT - VISITING DELEGATIONS ARRIVE IN 5 DAYS**

At the bottom of the notice, a red student council seal burned with clean authority.

**Emergency movement protocols authorized by Student Council President Rhea Valmont.**

The line was small. The reaction to it was not.

Two Red Circle students near the fountain stopped arguing mid-sentence and stepped out of the walkway. A cluster of Blue Circle candidates lowered their voices without an instructor telling them to. Even the floating notice crystals adjusted their height to keep the council seal visible above the crowd.

Aira followed my gaze.

Aira: "President Valmont does not usually attach her name to logistics unless she expects people to behave badly."

Cassian gave a short laugh.

Cassian: "Or unless she expects them to survive behaving badly."

Leon frowned.

Leon: "You know her?"

Cassian: "Every Red Circle heir knows Rhea Valmont. Some because they admire her. Most because they have been corrected by her in language their parents could not legally argue with."

I remembered the Red Circle student council president watching me after Leon's first defeat, her smile precise enough to feel like a blade placed flat against glass. So she had not vanished after noticing the thread. She had simply been standing where authority stood best: slightly ahead of disaster.

Below it appeared the list of confirmed competing institutions and the names of several high-profile student champions already known across the continent.

The campus reaction was immediate. Excitement rose, nerves sharpened, and status suddenly had teeth. Students crowded the notices, identifying famous names, rumored prodigies, and rival academy legends.

Aurelis's own team picks were no longer just talk. Time had become short.

Aira scanned the projected roster with growing dread.

Aira: "This is worse than I thought."

Haru: "You say that often."

Aira: "Because life keeps validating me."

She pointed at the list.

Aira: "Look. Valemere has registered **Soren Ashvale**, the Red Circle duelist with six consecutive academy titles. Drakenshard is fielding **Mara Kest**, that battlefield monster everyone keeps politely calling disciplined. And Noctis Dominion is sending..."

She went silent.

That silence did more than the names before it.

Soren Ashvale had earned whispers of admiration. Mara Kest had earned nervous laughter. Noctis Dominion earned space.

The students packed around the notice did not all stop talking at once. Instead, conversations thinned in uneven layers. A group of Blue Circle candidates pretended to study Valemere's roster while their eyes kept sliding back to the black Noctis crest. Two Red Circle heirs exchanged looks and said nothing. A Green support student near the edge of the crowd took one step backward without realizing it.

Even the projected banners above the courtyard seemed less bright around Noctis' name, swallowed rather than dimmed.

I had heard of Noctis Dominion College before coming to Aurelis. Everyone had. It was not the kind of school people praised casually. They spoke of its discipline, its victory record, its severe training culture, its graduates who entered military offices, high courts, and private enforcement houses with smiles sharp enough to count as weapons.

Noctis did not produce many beloved heroes. It produced results.

Leon noticed where my gaze had gone.

Leon: "Their candidates don't break formation."

Cassian's smile dropped a notch.

Cassian: "No. They break other things."

Aira looked at him.

Aira: "That was not comforting."

Cassian: "It was not meant to be."

Elira had not moved.

That was the part that caught me.

Elira Vale could stand before faculty, nobles, duelists, gossip, and pressure without giving away anything she did not choose to reveal. Her composure was trained, chosen, and reinforced by a will stronger than most magic I had seen at Aurelis.

Now her stillness had changed from calm into containment. Whatever name waited after Noctis Dominion, Elira already knew its shape, and she was holding the memory in place so it would not touch anyone else before it had to.

Elira stepped closer to read. Her expression shifted slightly. That was enough to matter.

Haru: "Who?"

Elira answered quietly.

Elira: "**Lucien Voss.**"

Her fingers closed around the side of our group's crystal dispatch slate hard enough to scatter the edge light. The motion lasted only a heartbeat before she smoothed her grip flat again: composed, public, Yellow Circle perfect.

But I had seen it. Lucien's name did not frighten her like a rival; it struck something remembered.

Cassian, standing just behind us, gave a low whistle.

Cassian: "That's a problem."

Leon stepped half a pace closer beside us, staring at the slate with visible tension.

Leon: "Noctis actually sent him?"

Aira looked between them.

Aira: "That is too much collective discomfort for one name. Who is he?"

Elira's gaze remained on the slate.

Elira: "A Yellow Circle."

That alone quieted her. Elira continued.

Elira: "Noctis Dominion's top prodigy. Lightless magic. Unmatched up close. He's been called one of the most dangerous young magicians in the tournament circuit."

Cassian folded his arms.

Cassian: "Dangerous is the polite word."

Aira: "And the impolite one?"

Cassian: "Cruel."

Aira looked back at the slate, suddenly less theatrical.

Aira: "Noctis listed him as captain."

The roster unfolded beneath Lucien's name in smaller letters.

**Nera Vail - Blue Circle Binding**  
**Oric Sen - Blue Circle Binding**  
**Tovan Reiss - Red Circle Close Combat**  
**Cael Nox - Conduit Support**

The last entry sat lower than the others, almost like the projection itself had been told to make it less important.

The roster expanded into formation notes when Aira touched the corner of the crystal dispatch slate. Noctis' support pattern unfolded in thin pale lines.

Nera Vail occupied Lucien's right flank. The projection listed ice-and-water locks, joint pins, lane control, and emergency pressure cover. Efficient. Clean. Nothing decorative except the rings shown on both wrists, and even those were probably tools pretending to be jewelry.

Aira leaned closer despite herself.

Aira: "Their support specialist is good."

Leon: "You can tell from a roster?"

Aira: "No. I can tell from what the roster does not bother explaining. See how every trap path assumes she'll adjust right after Lucien moves? That is not a weak support caster. That is someone trusted to make his cruelty look like strategy."

Under Nera's name, Oric Sen's lines mirrored hers with shorter reach and tighter backup guard. Then Cael's route appeared. Not beside Lucien. Through him.

Aira's mouth flattened.

Aira: "That is not a teammate diagram."

Elira's voice stayed quiet.

Elira: "No."

The slate display flickered once, showing a practice still from Noctis' qualifying match. Nera stood with one hand extended, blue-gray eyes fixed forward while ice-bindings sealed off a dangerous hallway. Behind Lucien, Cael's shoulders were drawn up too tight. Nera's gaze had shifted toward him by the smallest fraction.

Then Lucien's hand lifted in the still image. Nera faced forward again.

Haru: "She saw it."

Aira: "And continued."

Haru: "Yes."

Aira's expression turned sharper and less amused.

Aira: "I hate mirrors when they are people."

Leon frowned.

Leon: "Conduit support?"

Cassian's expression lost some of its humor.

Cassian: "Noctis likes power routes. A conduit takes strain so the main caster can push harder, longer, or through uglier angles."

Aira: "A terrible job, then."

Elira's voice was quiet.

Elira: "It can be, depending on who is allowed to say no."

The words did not sound theoretical.

Aira tapped the corner of the candidate slate again, advancing Noctis' public qualifying broadcast past the final buzzer into three unedited seconds of exit-tunnel footage before the tournament cameras cut away.

In the grain of the arena feed, Nera Vail turned toward the pale younger student as he stepped off the platform edge and lowered his casting arm. Even through tinny slate audio, her voice came out too clipped for tenderness.

Nera: "Your channels are strained. Report to medical before departure."

Cael's answer was too quiet for the crystal to catch. Nera's did not.

Nera: "I am not asking."

Oric Sen stood behind her in the doorway, unreadable. He did not help, and he did not stop her either.

The clip ended and snapped back to Lucien's portrait before the roster dimmed.

Small mercy, I thought, could still be fear wearing a uniform.

A second cold thread joined the first beneath my ribs. Lucien Voss was no longer only a name attached to Elira's history. He was a system walking toward us, wearing a student's face.

A breeze passed through the courtyard. Mana banners shifted overhead.

I watched Elira. There was something in her face I hadn't seen before. History, rather than simple fear.

Haru: "You know him."

She looked at me then, only for a second, and the answer was already there.

Elira: "A little."

Aira noticed immediately.

Aira: "How little is 'a little'?"

Elira's voice remained composed.

Elira: "Enough."

That was not enough for me. Not nearly.

Still, we were in the middle of the courtyard, surrounded by students, faculty, and rumor. This was not the place, not yet.

Something cold moved quietly under my ribs: protectiveness sharpening into focus. If Lucien Voss mattered to Elira's expression even that much, then he mattered to me already.

And I had a feeling the tournament was about to stop being merely competitive.

---

The name **Lucien Voss** followed us through the rest of the day.

It did not spread like ordinary gossip. Ordinary gossip moved quickly because people enjoyed it. Lucien's name moved carefully because people respected the danger attached to it.

By evening, every candidate in Aurelis knew Noctis Dominion College was sending its top Yellow Circle prodigy. Every hallway conversation carried fragments of the same uneasy facts: lightless affinity, close-range dominance, cruel.

Beneath all of that, the one detail that mattered most to me remained the one no one else could explain. Elira knew him.

Not well, she had said. Enough.

That word stayed with me longer than I wanted it to.

I did not ask her in the courtyard. That would have been careless: too many students, too many faculty eyes, too much rumor already turning every glance between us into a public event.

So I waited until the academy lights came on and the western garden paths grew quiet.

Elira stood beside me beneath a silver-leaf tree overlooking the lower city. The black necklace rested against her uniform, hidden beneath the appearance of a simple dark crystal pendant. To anyone else, it was pretty, lightly enchanted, harmless.

To me, it felt like a vow given shape.

Elira: "You've been quiet."

Haru: "That usually describes me."

Elira looked at me with the gentle patience of someone who had learned the difference between silence and hiding.

Elira: "Not like this."

I exhaled slowly.

Haru: "Lucien."

Her expression changed by less than a breath. Enough.

Elira turned toward the city lights below the cliff. For a few seconds, she watched the mana bridges glow in the distance as if the answer might be easier to give while looking at something far away.

Elira: "He was part of the junior tournament circuit two years ago."

Haru: "You fought him?"

Elira: "Not officially."

That answer sharpened my attention.

Elira: "Noctis Dominion hosted a youth exhibition. It was supposed to be controlled. Formal. Mostly political theater between schools."

Haru: "And it wasn't."

She shook her head once.

Elira: "Lucien fought a Blue Circle student from Valemere. His opponent was skilled, but clearly outmatched. The match should have ended after the first decisive lock."

Her hand moved unconsciously toward the pendant.
