Elira touched the ribbon with two fingers.

Elira: "Consent first."

Professor Valen: "Always, if the old builders were having a good century."

Humor lived in her voice, though not carelessness. Rhea's gaze sharpened.

President Valmont: "Can Noctis subpoena the house's record?"

Professor Valen closed the box and slid it into the advance supply pouch Rhea's courier was already buckling for the early wagon.

Professor Valen: "They may attempt to subpoena the lake if they enjoy humiliation."

Cassian's smile returned.

Cassian: "I want to watch that hearing."

Maelin: "No one is watching anything for forty-eight hours except meals, medicine, sleep, and whether Haru Aerlen remembers chairs exist for sitting rather than strategic door control."

I looked at her.

Maelin: "Do not test me. I have sedatives and moral clarity."

Elira laughed again, longer this time, and the ward-stone turned green. No one celebrated, because celebration asked too much of the hour. Yet Aira wrote a line in her notebook, and when I glanced over, I saw:

**Second laugh. Voluntary. Witnessed by friends, not systems.**

She noticed me looking and tilted the page toward me without hiding it.

Aira: "Some records are ours."

The sentence settled over the room more gently than any ward.

Rhea placed one more item on the table, not a document this time, but a small square of folded black cloth sealed with Aurelis blue and the plain white mark Senna Voss used for protected witness material. Elira's smile faded.

President Valmont: "Cael's public funeral record has been copied for the restoration house archive. Not the Council version. The Aurelis student version."

No one moved. The ward-stone in the bed frame hummed once, soft as a held breath.

Elira: "Why bring it here?"

Rhea kept her voice formal, the way she always kept tenderness intact in public.

President Valmont: "Because recovery leave is not exile from grief. And because Noctis filed a correction request at dawn."

Leon swore under his breath. Cassian's smile vanished. Aira's pen stopped.

Haru: "Correction?"

President Valmont: "They object to the phrase voluntary refusal of ownership. They prefer final service under catastrophic confusion."

The Black Circle did not rise. It went colder, which was worse. Elira's fingers tightened around mine until it hurt, and the pain kept me anchored in the room.

Elira: "No."

One quiet, wounded word, completely alive. Rhea inclined her head.

President Valmont: "The correction was denied. Mira's gallery copy, Nera's testimony, Darian's dissent, and Iven Sahl's funeral presence all support the existing language."

Elira looked at the folded cloth.

Elira: "Iven?"

President Valmont: "He asked if students from Noctis may sign the Aurelis copy without being absorbed into Noctis' official delegation."

Aira's eyes filled before she could blink them sharp.

Aira: "Good."

Leon: "Is he safe?"

President Valmont: "As safe as a Noctis student publicly refusing convenient language can be, which is to say not enough. Senna Voss has opened a protected channel."

Elira closed her eyes. For a moment I thought the news would push her back under the weight of the funeral. Instead she opened them and looked at Rhea.

Elira: "Send him my thanks."

President Valmont: "As Elira Vale or as primary witness?"

Elira's jaw tightened, then steadied.

Elira: "As Elira."

Professor Valen's sharp eyes softened. Maelin pretended to adjust the chart. Aira wrote the answer down. I wanted to memorize the way Elira said her own name there, stripped of title and function, and hated that memorizing it felt like another record. So I did not turn it into a monument. I only held her hand.

Rhea folded the cloth into the same advance courier pouch beside Valen's cedar box, Aira's supply hamper, and two sealed personal envelopes Mira and Iven had asked the courier runner to include.

President Valmont: "The copy and letters will ride ahead on the supply wagon and wait at the house if you request them. They will not present themselves otherwise."

Elira breathed in slowly.

Elira: "Thank you."

Cassian leaned against the wall, quieter than usual.

Cassian: "Cael would have hated all this paperwork."

Leon glanced sideways at him.

Cassian: "What? He had taste."

For one second, grief made room for the boy who had hated paperwork, not just the symbol around which it gathered. Elira's mouth trembled.

Elira: "He would have corrected the grammar."

Aira wiped at one eye with the back of her wrist and glared at her notebook as if ink had betrayed her.

Aira: "Then we will correct it for him."

When the carriage arrived, I helped Elira stand. She hated needing help, and I knew because she let me see that too.

Haru: "Tell me if I am holding too tightly."

Elira: "You are."

I loosened my grip at once. She did not pull away.

Elira: "Better."

Maelin brought the wheeled chair herself, both hands on the handles and a stare that dared any clerk, aide, or spectator to turn medical equipment into symbolism. Elira looked at the chair, then at the ward entrance beyond it. The hallway was not long. It only felt long because every door between the bed and the carriage had learned how to become public.

Maelin: "You may ride."

Elira: "May?"

Maelin's mouth tightened.

Maelin: "Medical permission. Not command."

Elira nodded once, then set one hand on the bed rail and pushed herself upright. Every person in the room tensed without stepping. Rhea's seal brightened. Leon shifted half a pace. I nearly moved toward the door. Elira caught all of it.

Elira: "No."

The word stopped us cleaner than a ward. She breathed through the first wave of dizziness, her hand shaking on the rail while the pendant at her throat stayed dark.

Elira: "I will use the chair if I need it."

Maelin studied her face.

Maelin: "You need it."

Elira: "Probably."

There was no theatrical defiance in it, which was why everyone listened.

Elira: "But I want to walk the first door."

Aira's pen lowered. Elira looked at me then.

Elira: "Beside me."

She did not add the second half aloud, and did not have to. I stepped to her side instead of the doorway. It took visible effort, and I was glad she could see the effort instead of wondering where I had hidden the fear.

Haru: "Beside you."

Elira placed her hand on my sleeve rather than my wrist, leaving one layer of cloth between skin and panic.

Rhea opened the ward door. The corridor beyond was lined with students, healers, council aides, and faculty pretending badly that they had not gathered into a farewell. The wheeled chair followed behind us like a patient argument. Elira took one step, then another. Nobody applauded, which was a mercy; applause would have made survival sound finished.

At the first doorframe, Elira stopped. Her breath had gone thin, sweat damp at her temple. Maelin brought the chair close without triumph, and Elira sat before her knees could make the decision for her.

Maelin: "Good."

Elira: "Do not sound pleased."

Maelin: "I am pleased by correct use of medical equipment. It is a private joy."

A small laugh moved through the doorway and broke nothing.

Rhea glanced down the corridor.

President Valmont: "Departure terms?"

Elira's fingers tightened once on my sleeve, then released.

Elira: "No procession."

Aira wrote it down.

Elira: "No applause. No one says brave."

Through the doorway, Mira Castellan hugged a sign board to her chest and nodded as if taking orders from someone who had earned the right to keep them small.

Elira: "If anyone asks what this is, say I am leaving before I become useful to the wrong people again."

The sentence entered the hallway plain and jagged, and it held. Rhea's council seal wrote the terms in red light beside the door.

**DEPARTURE BY STUDENT TERMS**

**NO PROCESSION**

**NO APPLAUSE**

**NO COURAGE CLAIM WITHOUT ACTOR CONSENT**

Mira copied the last line with both hands.

I thought of Elira waking with both hands at her throat. I thought of Cael lying under Rhea's seal. I thought of every instinct in me that wanted to build a wall between her and the watching world, and then I walked beside the chair. Beside. Not around.

At the outer ward entrance, the academy had gathered despite the notice forbidding a public send-off. Students stood in messy rows with notebooks, flowers, ribbons, and quiet faces. Mira held her sign high enough to see over the front row:

**RECOVERY IS NOT ABSENCE**

Beside her stood Iven Sahl, flanked by the Noctis students who had refused the official delegation. His hands were empty, his head bowed. Elira saw him and caught her breath, then lifted one hand in a greeting too small to be mistaken for a speech. Iven looked up as if someone had handed back his name.

The carriage door opened. Elira paused on the step.

Elira: "Haru."

Haru: "Yes?"

Elira: "When we get there, I do not want the first thing we do to be checking wards."

Every instinct in me objected. I swallowed all of them.

Haru: "What do you want first?"

She looked toward the lake road beyond the academy gates, where sunlight moved through trees untouched by trial halls, witness rails, and funeral banners.

Elira: "Tea."

Her fingers found mine.

Elira: "And then I want to sit somewhere no one is waiting for me to prove I survived correctly."

The Black Circle quieted beneath my ribs, attentive rather than coiled.

Haru: "Then tea first."

Elira stepped into the carriage, and I followed. Behind us, Aurelis did not cheer. The students stayed on the steps as the wheels began to roll, watching two people leave the center of the world because one of them had asked for quiet and the other had finally understood that quiet could be protection too.

## The Restoration House at Lake Velis

The restoration house did not look important enough to survive history. That was its first mercy.

It stood on the eastern shore of Lake Velis, tucked between cedar trees and a long slope of silver grass. The roof was dark green tile, the walls pale stone warmed by years of sun. No towers. No banners. No witness rail waiting to turn pain into testimony. Just windows. Too many windows for my comfort.

Elira noticed before the carriage stopped.

Elira: "You are counting entry points."

Haru: "No."

She looked at me.

Haru: "Yes."

I met her gaze without looking away. Elira leaned back against the carriage cushion, tired but amused.

Elira: "Tea first."

I exhaled.

Haru: "Tea first."

Professor Valen had left the front door unlocked after her dawn inspection, which nearly made me turn the carriage around. A note waited on the small entry table beneath a vase of white lake flowers.

**Small rebellions begin with entering without permission.**

Tucked beside it on the lid of a blue tin, in Aira's handwriting sent ahead on the early supply wagon:

**I told Professor Valen to check for traps, not beat me to the first joke. There are buns inside. Do not become tragic before eating.**

Elira read both notes and pressed a hand over her mouth. The laugh came out thin, but it came out.

The cedar box Professor Valen had sent ahead from the ward sat beside the vase. The black ribbon edged in silver waited inside, plain enough to look harmless and old enough that the air around it refused modern categories. Elira opened the lid and stood looking down at it.

Haru: "You do not have to decide now."

She touched the ribbon with two fingers.

Elira: "Yes, I do."

The answer was quiet, yet the house heard it. A line of old silver warmed along the entry table, then paused, waiting without impatience. Elira lifted the ribbon.

Haru: "Door or wrist?"

She looked toward the hall, then toward the lake-bright windows, then down at her own hands.

Elira: "Door first."

The choice surprised me, and she saw that too.

Elira: "If I tie it to my wrist immediately, someone will make it about whether I consent to being watched. If I tie it to the door, the first thing this house learns is that the room is chosen."

She moved to the inside of the front door and tied the ribbon through the small iron ring beneath the latch. Slowly, fumbling the first pass because her fingers were still weak. I kept my hands at my sides. She untangled the knot herself, breathed once, and tried again. The second knot held.

The house answered without ceremony. The floor warmed beneath our boots and wrote, in no language I had learned and every language my body understood:

**ENTERED BY CHOICE**

Elira's shoulders dropped, not all the way, just enough.

Elira: "Good."

Haru: "Good house."

The entry table gave a small wooden creak. Elira looked up at me.

Elira: "Did you just praise architecture?"

Haru: "It behaved well."

Her laugh came back, still unsteady, still hers. I lifted the satchel from her shoulder before she could pretend it was light, and she let me.

The house smelled of cedar, old paper, lake wind, and sugar. In the kitchen, a kettle warmed itself over a blue flame with no modern Circle signature. Old house magic from before the Circle ranks, humming without asking what I was.

Elira sat at the small table near the window while sunlight touched her hair. For one suspended breath, the kitchen forgot white healing gowns, funeral flowers, and the moment her gold had gone out in my arms.

Then a spoon clicked against porcelain.

Elira flinched.

The Black Circle rose so fast the window glass darkened at the edges.

Elira: "No."

One word, commanding without sharpness or fear. I froze with my hand half lifted.

The Black Circle did not understand a spoon. It understood sudden blows, incoming attacks, killing strikes, and the exact instant a room became too late. A porcelain click did not fit any category it trusted, so it invented one: sudden sound, Elira flinching, threat.

No. Neither Noctis nor Lucien, neither blade nor trap, only a kitchen beside a lake, sunlight on the wood, and cooling tea because both of us had forgotten normal things required unsteady human hands.

The power did not believe me. I could read ancient wards and stop a spell mid-flight, yet I could not explain safety to the part of me built out of every second I had failed to keep her safe. For a heartbeat, I felt how easy it would be to force the whole house silent. No sharp sounds. No sudden motion. A perfect quiet arranged around her fear.

The thought sickened me because it arrived dressed as care. I held my hand still in midair while the kettle flame bent away from me.

Elira breathed once, twice, her knuckles white around the table edge.

Elira: "It was just the sound."

Haru: "I know."

Elira: "You did not know. You reacted."

That was true, and unbearable.

Haru: "I'm sorry."

Elira closed her eyes.

Elira: "Please do not apologize like you have already retreated."

I lowered my hand. The window glass cleared.

Haru: "What do you need?"

Elira opened her eyes, wet and steady.

Elira: "For you to sit down."

I sat across from her. She looked at the empty chair beside her own, so I moved there instead. A few inches of old floorboard separated the chairs, and crossing them felt harder than walking into a hearing room.

Elira reached for the spoon. Her hand shook. I kept both hands on my knees and did not take it from her. That cost more restraint than holding back a spell.

She stirred her tea slowly. The spoon clicked again, softer. She flinched again, less. I stayed seated, keeping the Black Circle locked beneath my skin.

Elira watched me as carefully as I watched her.

Elira: "Again."

Haru: "You don't have to..."

Elira: "I know."

She stirred once more. Click. Her breath caught, then let go. Outside the window, the lake moved in slow silver lines.

Elira: "There."

Haru: "There."

She looked down into the cup.

Elira: "I do not want my fear to become another thing everyone organizes around."

Haru: "Fear deserves care."

Elira: "Yes. Not a throne."

That sounded so much like her that something tight in my chest loosened enough to ache. I reached slowly, keeping my hand in sight until she turned her palm up.

We drank tea and ate Aira's buns from the blue tin. Elira managed half of one and declared victory. I ate three because she watched me with narrowed eyes until I stopped pretending I did not need food.

After tea, the house began introducing itself through small refusals.

When I walked toward the largest window to inspect the latch, the floorboards warmed under my boots and traced a line of silver in the wood.

**GUEST.**

No voice. No chime. Just a clear impression that rejected asset, candidate, and Black Circle in favor of one plain word. I stared down at my boots.

Elira, pulling her coat snugly around her shoulders on the cushioned kitchen window bench, watched me over her cup.

Elira: "Did the floor just scold you?"

Haru: "It identified me."

Elira's brows drew together.

Haru: "As a guest."

She was silent for a moment, and then relief touched her face, cautious and shy of trusting itself.

Elira: "Good house."

The floor cooled, apparently satisfied. I considered thanking it aloud and stopped myself. That was already a dangerous degree of cooperation with furniture.

Elira set her cup down and looked toward the hallway.

Elira: "Show me the rest?"

Haru: "Maelin said stairs only if necessary."

Elira waited.

Haru: "The rest of the first floor."

Elira: "Better."

We moved slowly. At Aurelis, slowness had meant timing and discipline. Here it meant her hand resting against the plaster wall when the room tilted, or stopping between the kitchen and the sitting room while her breath caught for no reason either of us could name.

Haru: "Stop?"

Elira nodded once. I did not reach for her; she curled her fingers around my sleeve, taking the measure of help through cloth.

Elira: "It is annoying."

Haru: "The weakness?"

Elira's eyes narrowed. I heard my mistake before Maelin could materialize in spirit and strike me with a clipboard.

Haru: "No. I mean your body needing time to catch up. Not weakness."

Elira let me sweat for three seconds.

Elira: "Acceptable correction."

Haru: "Thank you."

Elira: "Barely."

The corner of her mouth twitched. Second victory of the afternoon.

The sitting room faced the lake through three tall windows. White curtains stirred in a breeze with no clear source. A low shelf held blankets, board games, blank notebooks, a small music box, and six sealed packets Aira had packed onto the advance wagon with strict placement notes for the house staff.

**FOR WHEN HARU LOOKS LIKE HE IS ABOUT TO INVENT A PROTOCOL.**

Elira picked up the first packet. Inside was a deck of hand-painted cards and a slip of paper:

**Play something with rules you did not write.**

The second packet held dried peach slices.

**Feed him. Feed yourself first, because hierarchy matters.**

The third held a small blue ribbon.

**Emergency hair management. Do not ask Leon for help unless you want one side battle-ready and the other side tragic.**

Elira laughed softly. The sound still surprised her, and surprised me too, though I stayed quiet and listened without trying to trap it.

Elira ran her thumb over the ribbon.

Elira: "She was scared."

Haru: "Aira?"

Elira nodded.

Elira: "This is what she does when she is scared. She builds logistics so no one has to say the frightening part first."

I thought of Aira's notebook in the ward room.

Haru: "It works."

Elira looked at me with tired affection.

Elira: "On you especially."

I could not deny it.

Beyond the sitting room lay a small study. Professor Valen had left that door unlocked too, and the desk faced the inner wall rather than the lake, as if she understood that someone turned into a public spectacle sometimes needed a wall promising nothing could walk up behind her.

Three folders lay on the blotter: one blue, one red, one plain brown. Elira's fingers tightened on my sleeve.

Haru: "We do not have to open them."

Elira: "What are they?"

I checked the seals without touching them.

Haru: "Medical instructions. Council contact conditions. Personal letters."

Elira stared at the brown folder.

Elira: "Personal from whom?"

The floorboards nudged the corner of the brown folder half an inch closer to her. I disliked how much personality this building had. Elira caught my expression.

Elira: "It likes me better."

Haru: "Everyone does."

Her face softened quickly enough that I did not regret saying it.

She opened the brown folder. The first letter was from Mira Castellan, careful at the top and growing breathless by the second paragraph. Elira read silently, her eyes slowing near the middle.

Elira: "She says the Green Circle students are not copying the sequence because they think I owe them proof."

She swallowed hard.

Elira: "They are copying it because they do not want anyone turning Cael's death into a rumor before the record can protect him."

Outside, wind moved through the cedar needles.

Haru: "Mira understands records."

Elira: "She understands grief."

I had no answer to that.

The second letter lay on unsigned Noctis paper with no official seal. Elira hesitated.

Haru: "I can read it first."

Elira's mouth pressed thin.

Elira: "No."

She drew a steadying breath and touched my elbow.

Elira: "But sit close."

I pulled up the second chair and sat beside her.

Iven Sahl's letter-delivered ahead in Rhea's courier pouch-was short and clumsy. He wrote that Cael had once lent him a thermal charm during winter drills and told him not to give it back until his hands stopped shaking-words Iven wrote he only understood at the funeral, when he stopped confusing obedience with survival. He wrote that he had not understood then, and was beginning to now. At the bottom, one line had been crossed out and written again.

**I am sorry he had to die where we could finally see him.**

Elira pressed her hand over her mouth. No laugh came this time, only shaky, careful breathing. I let my shoulder touch hers, and she leaned into it.

Elira: "He should not have to apologize to me."

Haru: "No."

Elira: "Noctis made children write grief like petitions."

The Black Circle stirred beneath my ribs, pulled not toward the windows, but toward Noctis itself: frightened students, neat forms, and polite murder. Elira's hand found mine under the desk.

Elira: "Beside me."

I drew one slow breath, then another.

Haru: "Beside you."

We left the red and blue folders shut. It felt like treason against urgency, and like keeping the first promise of the day.

Later, we wandered back into the kitchen because Elira wanted to look at the buns again. She inspected them with the solemn gravity of a commander reviewing troops.

Elira: "That one has too much sugar."

Haru: "For whom?"

Elira: "For dignity."

Haru: "Dignity survived Lucien. It can survive icing."

She looked sideways at me.

Haru: "Aira has been affecting my speech."

Elira: "Good."

She picked the smallest bun and took two bites. Victory revised upward.

Afterward she insisted on walking to the back threshold, not outside yet, where cedar shade met the pale stone step and Lake Velis spread beyond the grass like a piece of sky laid down to rest. Elira stood with one hand braced on the doorframe while wind lifted her hair. Her pendant hung still against her collar, looking for one quiet minute like an ordinary stone chosen for beauty.

Elira: "I thought I would feel safer here."

Haru: "Do you?"

She studied the water.

Elira: "No."

My hand tightened at my side. She saw it at once.

Elira: "Not because the house failed. Because safety is not something a place can hand back all at once."

The words made sense. I disliked them anyway.

Elira: "But I feel less watched."

Haru: "There are wards."

Elira: "Wards are not the same as eyes."

The threshold warmed beneath our soles, approving or offended; it was hard to tell. Elira stepped back inside before I could suggest she was tired, then promptly ruined my restraint by swaying once. I caught her elbow, visible and careful. She leaned into the support and shut her eyes.

Elira: "I hate that I needed that."

Haru: "I know."

Elira: "Do not say you are sorry."

Haru: "I was not going to."

She opened one eye.

Haru: "I was going to say I am glad I was beside you."

Her expression softened. She let the sentence stand, and let me walk her back to the sitting-room sofa.

By late afternoon, the security perimeter checked in through the front hall mirror. Rhea's council seal flared in the glass first.

President Valmont: "Status."

From the sofa under her blanket, Elira raised her teacup.

Elira: "Tea achieved."

Rhea blinked once.

President Valmont: "Acceptable."

Aira shoved her face into the reflection beside Rhea's shoulder.

Aira: "That is not an update. Are there chairs? Are there blankets? Has Haru threatened a shrub?"

Haru: "No."

Elira: "He considered the windows."

Aira: "Progress. Windows are not shrubs."

Leon appeared behind them with his arms folded.

Leon: "The eastern road is clear. Two Council outriders passed an hour ago. No Noctis relay interference."

Cassian leaned into frame from the other side.

Cassian: "Also, Dren says if Aerlen cracks the restoration house, he has to repair it without celestial shortcuts."

Haru: "Noted."

Elira's smile faded as she studied their faces.

Elira: "How is Aurelis?"

The mirror quieted. Aira answered first.

Aira: "Messy. Awake. Too many committees. Too many people pretending they always believed mercy was policy."

Leon: "Green Circle students are still copying the public sequence records."

Cassian: "Noctis pulled its official banner from the east dormitory. The student group stayed."

President Valmont: "High Councilor Krail filed another risk warning at noon."

Elira's fingers tightened around her cup. I felt the tension before she spoke.

Haru: "About me?"

President Valmont: "About your proximity to every major witness, yes. Senna Voss marked it procedurally premature."

Aira: "Which is formal language for sit down and stop pointing at grieving students."

President Valmont: "Less colorful, but accurate."

Elira set her cup down.

Elira: "Do not keep all of it from us."

Professor Valen stepped into the reflection then, her gaze gentle enough to be dangerous.

Professor Valen: "We will not. But recovery leave is not remote command. You are allowed to hear the news without solving it before supper."

Elira looked ready to argue, then exhaustion slid across her face.

Elira: "I hate how reasonable that is."

Aira: "Excellent. Hate it while resting."

The mirror dimmed once Rhea set the morning check-in time, leaving the house quiet and ours for the evening.

## The Spoon Test

Before we went down the hall to look at bedrooms for the night, Elira decided supper should include hot soup.

That was not one of Maelin's directives. Maelin had sent jars of broth and written instructions ahead on the infirmary supply wagon with the grim satisfaction of a healer who believed nourishment could overrule shock by sheer stubbornness. Elira's decision was smaller, and far less polite to grief.

She insisted on holding the spoon herself.

At the kitchen table, her hand shook before the spoon even cleared the bowl. I noticed before she lifted it, because I noticed everything that looked like struggle or harm. My fingers twitched half an inch off the wood to steady her wrist, then stopped.

Elira: "Let me fail once before you rescue me."

The words cut deep. She saw that they did, and did not take them back.

The spoon reached her mouth on the second try, awkwardly, spilling a warm streak of broth across the towel spread over her knees. Aira would have logged it as soup aggression.

Elira let out one short laugh that startled both of us. I stared at the wet stain on her lap as if it were an unruly miracle.

Elira: "There. Alive."

I let out a long breath, something tight beneath my ribs giving way at last. For that minute, no council owned the word.

After I carried the soup bowls to the sink, I noticed the advance infirmary orderlies had prepared two bedrooms at the far end of the first-floor hall according to Maelin's packing list.

The larger room faced the lake. A smaller one waited across the corridor with its door open, blankets turned down, and a self-igniting lamp warm on the sill. Fresh clothes had been split evenly between both rooms rather than laid out like orders.

On the larger room's bedside table sat a sealed note in Maelin's neat hand, packed that morning after watching my chair vigil in the ward.

**The patient sleeps worse alone. The proximity witness destabilizes when exiled to chairs. Two beds exist. Use one or both. Ask each other instead of inventing a medical doctrine about it.**

Elira read it twice. Color rose in her cheeks that had nothing to do with fever, and she handed the paper to me.

Elira: "She anticipated both of us badly."

Haru: "Accurately."

Elira: "Unfortunately."

I glanced toward the open door across the hall.

Haru: "I can sleep there."

Elira: "I know."

Haru: "I don't want to assume."

Her expression softened, then tightened with the simple effort of staying upright.

Elira: "Then ask before I fall asleep in this hallway and make the decision medically embarrassing."

Haru: "Do you want me beside you?"

Elira's hand rose to the pendant. This time she did not grip it. She only rested two fingers over the crystal, as if reminding herself it was present without being the whole story.

Elira: "Yes."

Her answer was quiet and certain.

Elira: "I am scared to sleep. I am more scared to wake and have to search for you."

My throat closed.

Haru: "Then I will be beside you."

Elira: "Not guarding the door."

Haru: "Beside you."

She nodded once.

That night, the house taught us how awkward ordinary survival could be. Elira changed behind the folding screen while I stared out at the lake with the grim focus of someone studying enemy formations. She caught me at it and laughed under her breath, which made both of us blush worse than the moment deserved.

When I came back from the washroom, she was sitting on the bed in a pale blue sleeping robe, her hair loose over one shoulder, the dark pendant resting against the cloth.

Seeing her simply alive undid me. Elira saw it in my face.

Elira: "Come here."

I did, slowly. She shifted under the blanket, and at first I lay down on top of the spare coverlet, because apparently even after everything I could still manage to be ridiculous.

Elira stared up at the ceiling.

Elira: "Haru."

Haru: "Yes?"

Elira: "Are you planning to sleep like a formal apology?"

I turned my head toward her. Her mouth trembled, and mine did too.

Haru: "I am trying to be respectful."

Elira: "I know."

She reached under the edge of the blanket and found my hand.

Elira: "Respect me by believing I can choose closeness."

The Black Circle warmed once beneath my ribs, steady and quiet. I moved beneath the covers only when she tugged my hand, settling shoulder against shoulder until warmth met warmth. She exhaled as if she had been holding that breath since the Wounded City.

For a while, we listened to the lake against the shore.

Elira: "Aira is going to call this a honeymoon."

I blinked into the dim room.

Haru: "This is medical leave."

Elira: "That will not stop her."

Haru: "No."

Elira's fingers tightened around mine.

Elira: "Would it be terrible if part of me wanted it to feel a little like one?"

The question entered me more carefully than any blade. I turned toward her.

Haru: "No."

Her eyes caught the low lamplight.

Haru: "It would be human."

She looked at me for a long moment, then rested her forehead against my shoulder.

Elira: "I want some part of being alive to belong to love. Not councils. Not Noctis. Not death. Us."

My hand rose to her hair and paused a fraction of an inch away. She leaned into the pause, giving permission again. I stroked her hair once, then again, slow enough for both of us to believe it.

Haru: "Then tomorrow belongs to us."

Elira: "Not all of it."

Haru: "No. Not all."

Elira: "But enough."

Outside, moonlight moved across the lake. Inside, Elira fell asleep with her hand in mine. I stayed awake longer, listening to her breathe without counting, letting the quiet hold through the night.

===== EPISODE 16 =====

# Episode 16: **The Quiet Place**

The night after the spoon test did not heal us.

It gave us a morning.

The first full day at Lake Velis began with Elira stealing my shirt.

That was not how she described it.

Elira: "This was folded on the wrong chair."

Haru: "It was folded on my chair."

She stood in the bedroom doorway wearing the dark shirt over her pale sleeping robe, sleeves falling past her wrists, hair loose and gold in the morning light.

Elira: "Then your chair made a generous decision."

I had faced Lucien's lightless pressure, old Foundation systems, Dominion Severance, public ranking, and the Black Circle trying to become grief with a shape.

None of them prepared me for Elira Vale looking warm, tired, and pleased with herself in my shirt.

She noticed. Of course she did.

Elira: "You are staring."

Haru: "Yes."

I did not bother pretending otherwise.

Her confidence faltered for half a breath, caught between wanting to be looked at and remembering how lately every stare had been medical, political, or mournful. I saw the moment she wondered whether my eyes were finding the wound before the woman.

So I gave her the truth plainly, leaving nothing out.

Haru: "You look like you slept. You look annoyed that you needed to. You look beautiful. The shirt is not getting returned, is it?"

The uncertainty left her face.

Elira: "Absolutely not."

After a brisk two-minute dawn check-in on the hall mirror-satisfied once Elira raised her teacup and signed Maelin's pulse strip-breakfast was bread, fruit, soft cheese, and another note from Aira tucked inside the jam cupboard.

**If this note is found by Haru: make her eat something. If found by Elira: make him eat something. If found by both: I am excellent at friendship.**

Elira read it aloud with solemn dignity.

Then she ate two slices of bread because Aira's threat carried across distance.

Afterward, we walked to the lake. Slowly. Elira hated the slowly.

Her body betrayed it in small ways: a pause at the porch steps, a hand tightening on the railing, measuring her breath too carefully when the path sloped downward. She did not complain. That made it worse.

At the third pause, I stopped beside her.

Haru: "You can be angry."

Elira looked at the lake instead of me.

Elira: "I am."

Haru: "At me?"

Elira: "Sometimes."

The answer landed cleanly. I nodded.

Haru: "Good."

She turned then.

Elira: "Good?"

Haru: "If you are angry at me, you are not making yourself grateful for every breath."

Her eyes sharpened. Then softened.

Elira: "That was annoyingly sharp."

Haru: "Aira has been a bad influence."

Elira: "Aira would call it a good influence loudly enough to be heard from Aurelis."

We continued down the path.

At the waterline, an old wooden dock stretched over the lake. The boards had been repaired many times by practical hands. No ceremony. No crest marks. Just care repeated until it held together.

Elira sat at the edge and removed her shoes. I sat beside her. For several minutes, we let our feet hover above the water like cowards.

Elira: "It is going to be cold."

Haru: "Probably."

Elira: "You first."

Haru: "A command from the Yellow Circle prodigy?"

Elira: "A request from your recovery-leave girlfriend."

I put my feet in the water.

Cold shot up my legs so fast my entire soul reconsidered loyalty.

Elira laughed fully, clear and startled, one hand pressed to her chest as if the sound had surprised her too.

The Black Circle stirred in answer, warm for once instead of watchful.

Elira lowered her feet into the lake.

Her laugh broke into a gasp.

Elira: "That is cruel."

Haru: "The lake?"

Elira: "You, for not warning me enough."

Haru: "I suffered visibly."

Elira: "You suffer quietly. It is one of your worst habits."

The water moved around our ankles. Sunlight scattered across the surface in broken gold. For once, gold did not look like a classification. It looked like morning. Elira's shoulder touched mine.

Elira: "Tell me something ordinary."

Haru: "Ordinary?"

Elira: "Something you like. Just because it is yours, not because it serves a plan or proves some old rule."

I thought too long. She bumped my shoulder.

Elira: "That delay was tragic."

Haru: "I like rain on stone."

Elira's expression gentled.

Elira: "Why?"

Haru: "It makes large places sound less empty."

She absorbed that without turning it into pity.

Elira: "I like pear jam."

Haru: "Because?"

Elira: "Because when I was little, my mother insisted proper Vale breakfasts meant self-control, and my father would put too much pear jam on toast when she looked away."

Haru: "A family rebellion."

Elira: "A sticky one."

We traded ordinary things until noon.

Rain on stone. Pear jam. The smell of old paper. The way Aira said "interesting" when she meant "this is a disaster." Leon pretending not to care about compliments. Cassian's habit of smiling before doing something risky. Professor Valen's dry half-smile when she was three moves ahead of an argument. Maelin's war against nonsense. Lake birds stepping like officials over the mud.

Each small thing made the world wider than catastrophe.

Then a bell rang from the house. Elira's hands quieted. The lake was gone from her eyes.

She was back under public relays, somewhere between her own choice and the route that had killed her.

I did not stand. I wanted to. Every part of me wanted to find the bell, smash the thing, silence every sound shaped like warning.

Instead I stayed beside her.

Haru: "Lake."

Her fingers dug into the dock.

Haru: "Wood under your hands. Cold water. My shoulder next to yours."

Elira's breath came too fast.

Elira: "It sounded like the marker bell."

Haru: "I know."

Elira: "I am here."

Haru: "Yes."

I kept my eyes on hers and my voice low enough that she could still hear the water moving beneath the boards.

Elira: "I am not there."

Haru: "No."

She reached for my hand with a violence that was not aimed at me. I gave it. The Black Circle pressed behind my ribs, cold and old, tasting faintly of ozone and metal. Old systems recognized fear and wanted to contain it, rank it, make it useful.

I kept it quiet.

Elira's breathing slowed. When she looked at me again, shame had moved in behind the panic.

I hated shame more than fear.

Elira: "I was fine."

Haru: "You were scared."

Elira: "I was laughing ten minutes ago."

Haru: "Both can be true."

Her eyes filled.

Elira: "I do not know how to be both."

The ache in her voice had little to do with the bell. Someone had taught her that surviving meant choosing one clean shape and holding it until it broke.

I turned fully toward her on the dock.

Haru: "Then we practice."

Elira: "Practice?"

Haru: "Being both."

She stared at me. So I did the only useful thing I could think of.

I picked up a lake bird feather from the dock, held it with grave seriousness, and placed it on my knee.

Haru: "This is official practice."

Elira blinked.

Haru: "You are allowed to be frightened and also judge this feather."

Her mouth twitched.

Elira: "That feather is unimpressive."

Haru: "Harsh."

Elira: "It lacks structure."

Haru: "It survived a lake bird."

Elira: "A low standard."

The laugh came back through tears. It hurt to hear, and it healed nothing by itself, but it made room.

We dried our feet on the hem of my coat, put our shoes back on, and walked up the path to the house together.

By the time we stepped onto the porch, the bell had revealed itself as a delivery charm resting beside a wicker basket from Aurelis. We carried it inside to the kitchen counter. Rhea had sent documents sealed for later alongside a palm-sized folding check-in mirror wrapped in wool so Elira would not have to walk back to the entry hall for every call. Maelin had sent medicine. Aira had sent three more notes, each hidden in increasingly unreasonable places. Leon had sent a water-stabilizing charm with no message. Cassian had sent a red ribbon tied around a packet of spiced chocolate and a note that read:

**For morale. Deny everything.**

Elira held the chocolate like evidence.

Elira: "We are very loved."

Haru: "In ways that don't quite fit together."

She leaned against the kitchen counter, wrapped in my shirt and her shawl, and suddenly looked close to tears again.

Elira: "I did not know being loved could be exhausting."

Haru: "I think it is because you keep trying to answer it."

Elira: "What should I do instead?"

I opened my mouth. Then closed it. Correct answers had hurt her yesterday.

So I chose a true one.

Haru: "Let some of it sit beside you."

She looked at the basket. Then at me.

Elira: "Like you are learning to do?"

I accepted that.

Haru: "Like I am learning to do."

The basket stayed on the counter for an hour because neither of us wanted to decide what to do with kindness.

After the Wounded City, even small gifts arrived weighted with records, witness seals, protection clauses, and people bracing against the next loss.

A ribbon. A charm. Medicine. Chocolate. Documents sealed for later.

Elira touched Leon's water-stabilizing charm.

The charm was plain blue glass wrapped in a strip of cloth from an Aurelis training sleeve. Leon had tied the knot badly, in the specific way of someone who had tried very hard and gotten angry at string.

Elira: "He did not write a note."

Haru: "He would think that was overdoing it."

Elira turned the charm in her hand.

Elira: "He stayed with Cael when the field tried to make him into bait."

Haru: "Yes."

Elira: "And now he sends this with no words because words would admit he is worried."

Haru: "Also yes."

Her thumb moved over the knot.

Elira: "We should thank him."

Haru: "Aira will make him unbearable if she knows."

Elira's eyes warmed.

Elira: "Then we thank him privately."

The house, which had developed opinions about privacy, opened a drawer in the writing desk by half an inch. I looked at it.

Haru: "Stop helping."

Elira laughed. The drawer remained open. Inside were blank cards, a fountain pen, and envelopes already marked with old restoration-house seals that meant nothing to the Council and apparently everything to the road wards.

Elira picked up a card.

Her hand trembled before the pen touched paper.

This time it was only fatigue.

She scowled at the tremor as if it had insulted her family.

Haru: "I can write."

Elira: "I know."

She dipped the pen.

The first line came out slightly uneven.

**Leon, your charm is useful. Your knot is terrible. Thank you.**

She stared at it. Then looked at me.

Elira: "Too much?"

Haru: "He will understand the insult as affection."

Elira: "Good."

She added:

**Do not tell Aira I said so.**

We both knew Aira would know within an hour of the envelope leaving the house. Still, Elira's handwriting existed outside official testimony now, and Leon would probably stare at the card far too long before pretending he had not.

We wrote to Aira next.

That took longer because Aira deserved gratitude and also needed management. Elira began:

**Your packets are intrusive.**

Then paused.

Haru: "True."

Elira added:

**They helped.**

Her expression shifted.

Elira: "She will cry."

Haru: "Aira?"

Elira: "Privately. Then she will deny it with footnotes."

I imagined Aira making up an excuse about tactical eye moisture so she would not have to admit crying.

Haru: "Likely."

Elira wrote:

**You are excellent at friendship. This is not permission to become worse.**

We left space for me.

I did not know what to write.

Elira slid the card toward me without speaking.

The pen felt heavier than it should have.

Aira had been the first person at Aurelis to treat my silence as a thing with doors instead of walls. She had made maps around my omissions, jokes around fear, and a public record strong enough to keep the old systems from turning me into only a rank. I wrote:

**Thank you for making room before you knew what needed room.**

Then I stopped. The sentence looked exposed. Elira read it and did not rescue me from it.

She only touched the edge of the card.

Elira: "Good."

We wrote to Rhea in language formal enough to survive being intercepted and human enough to make her sigh.

We wrote to Maelin to confirm medicine had been taken, food had been eaten, and neither of us had turned the bedroom into a moral crisis. Elira insisted on that line. I objected with dignity. She ignored me with more.

We did not open the Council documents.

The red folder sat on the desk like a sealed wound.

At one point I reached toward it.

Elira did not stop me.

That made stopping myself harder.

My fingers hovered over the seal.

I could guess what the memos inside looked like. High Councilor Krail's words would be neat and careful. Words like stability, proximity, unranked exposure, necessary review. No open cruelty. Nothing as honest as a blade. Just concern arranged until it could justify a locked door.

The Black Circle disliked locked doors. So did I. That was why I pulled my hand back. Elira watched me.

Elira: "Why did you stop?"

Haru: "Because if I read it now, I will spend the afternoon answering a man who wants to make me react."

Elira's face softened.

Elira: "And what did you want to spend the afternoon doing?"

I looked at the basket. At the half-written cards. At the window where the lake kept being only a lake.

Haru: "Learning what people do with afternoons."

Elira set the pen down.

Elira: "That may be the most alarming thing you have ever said."

Haru: "I assumed there were procedures."

Elira: "There are not."

Haru: "None?"

Elira considered.

Elira: "Tea helps."

That was close enough to a rulebook. We made more tea. Elira insisted on helping, which meant I had to learn the difference between helping and hovering for the fourth time that day. She carried the cups one at a time. Slowly. Angrily. Successfully.

When she set mine down without spilling, she gave me a look so triumphant that the Black Circle itself seemed wise enough not to comment.

Haru: "Impressive."

Elira: "Do not sound surprised."

Haru: "I am impressed by the cup."

Elira: "Cruel."

Haru: "Accurate."

She threw a folded napkin at me.

It hit my shoulder and fell to the floor with no tactical effect.

Elira: "Devastating."

Haru: "I may not recover."

Her smile faltered once before returning, and that was enough for one afternoon.

The house accepted our letters at the front door.

There was a narrow brass slot beside the entry table. When Elira slid the envelopes through, the old silver in the wood brightened and the cards vanished into whatever route Professor Valen trusted more than council courier chains.

Elira kept one envelope back. Plain. Unsealed. Iven Sahl's name written on it.

Haru: "Do you want to wait?"

Elira looked down at the card.

Elira: "No. I want to not send a perfect answer."

She opened it again. Inside, she had written:

**Iven, you do not owe me an apology for surviving Noctis. Cael's kindness belonged to him. What you do with the part of it he gave you can belong to you. If you ever want to tell the thermal charm story into the public record, Rhea will protect the route. If you do not, that choice is also yours.**

Below it, after a gap:

**Eat something warm.**

I looked at her. Elira's cheeks colored.

Elira: "Aira has contaminated me."

Haru: "Good."

She sealed the letter before she could edit it into distance.

The house took that one more gently than the rest.

## Interlude: Elira's Kept Copy

Haru went to rinse the cups, giving her the quiet of an ordinary chore instead of hovering near the desk.

Elira let him go. Letting someone leave a room without bracing for the worst was harder than asking him to stay.

The restoration house settled around her in soft old creaks: cedar beams adjusting to lake wind, kettle cooling, ward lines humming beneath the floor. No council railing. No crowd of witnesses. No public record waiting to turn every breath into a legal rule.

Only the brass mail slot beside the door. It brightened again.

Elira looked toward the kitchen.

Haru had his back to her, sleeves rolled to his elbows, washing a cup with the focused care of a boy who could unmake a battlefield and still looked faintly uncertain about soap. The slot opened.

A folded crystal sheet slid onto the entry table.

It bore no hostile flare. No Noctis seal. No Dominion hook.

That almost made it worse.

Plain Council paper could do a lot of harm while pretending it was only asking a polite question. Elira picked it up.

**SUPPLEMENTAL WELFARE CONTEXT FORM**

**RECOVERY PROXIMITY REVIEW**

**OPTIONAL STUDENT RESPONSE**

Optional, in council language, often meant someone wanted refusal to look suspicious later.

She read the first question.

**Does Haru Aerlen's presence noticeably reduce your distress?**

Elira's fingers tightened around the page.

There it was: a corridor built one polished tile at a time, long before anyone said the word containment aloud.

If she answered yes, someone could call him necessary.

If she answered no, someone could call him irrelevant.

If she refused, someone could call the refusal evidence of dependency hidden by romance, grief, or Black Circle influence.

She could almost hear Krail's voice inside the grammar, though his name appeared nowhere. The trap was too tidy to need a signature.

Haru turned from the sink.

Haru: "Elira?"

She folded the sheet once.

Elira: "A form."

His hands stopped moving.

Anyone else would have missed it. She did not.

The pause behind his eyes. The quick sizing-up of danger, what a move would cost, whether the kinder thing was to step closer or give her the page to herself. He chose space. Good.

She did not want distance from him. She only wanted one answer that did not begin with his fear.

Elira: "I am going to read it first."

Haru set the washed cup on the drying rack and reached quietly for the kettle.

Haru: "All right."

He did not ask to see it. That helped.

It did not solve the anger.

Elira took the sheet to the small writing desk by the western window. The lake beyond the glass looked too peaceful for bureaucracy. That seemed unfair to the lake.

The form had seven questions. All gentle. All wrong.

**Does proximity to the Black Circle bearer produce measurable channel stability?**

Elira crossed out proximity. Wrote: **Chosen company.**

Then crossed out Black Circle bearer. Wrote: **Haru Aerlen.** The sentence became messier. Better.

**Does romantic attachment alter your willingness to provide testimony?**

Elira stared at that one longer.

She thought of the Wounded City. Black Dominion thread biting into her own wrist after she caught Cael's return hook; the dead gray line below his collarbone and Haru's later account of black threads knotting beneath Cael's wrists at the fountain. Haru's face when she pushed her gold shield outward and Dominion Severance turned protection into a blade.

Love had not blunted her willingness to testify. It had only made certain men furious that her testimony still belonged to her. She wrote:

**Caring about someone does not take away my free will. It only gives bad readers another excuse to doubt it.**

The pen trembled. She hated that.

Then she decided trembling could stay.

Mira would have kept it.

Mira would have written a note beside the line: **HAND SHOOK HERE. STILL ANSWERED.** Elira added it herself.

The page looked less elegant immediately. Good.

Elegance had been trained into her as a survival tool until it could hide pain behind poise. Mira had taught her that ugly records sometimes protected people better because they proved a living hand had made them under pressure.

Question five asked whether Haru's continued presence might get in the way of recovering on her own. Elira laughed once. It came out sharp.

Haru stayed quiet in the kitchen, rinsing the teapot slowly while giving her space. Still listening. She wrote:

**Recovering on my own: answering this without asking him to rescue me from the insult.**

Then, below it:

**I choose his company when I want it. I choose to be alone when I want that. Right now your form treats both choices as symptoms unless they give you the answer you want. Fix the test before you judge the patient.**

That was too Halden. She left it.

Question seven was the worst.

**Would you consent to a private medical-context interview to distinguish recovery need from personal preference?**

Private. Medical-context. Distinguish.

The words put on clean gloves before reaching for her throat.

Elira did not cross anything out this time.

She wrote beneath the question in large, uneven script:

**No private interview. No separation disguised as clarity. Needing help to heal and choosing who I care about are not opposites. If you want testimony, ask in an open hearing after the healers clear me. If you want control, stop pretending this is care.**

The house hummed around her, whether old cedar settling or old wards agreeing.

She rejected both Lady Elira Vale and Yellow Circle primary witness and signed the name she chose:

**Elira Vale. Student. Alive. Irritated.**

That last word was not proper. She underlined it.

Then she made a copy by hand before sending the crystal sheet through the brass slot, because Aira had contaminated everyone and because Mira would ask.

When the house took the form, Elira sat very still. She had expected relief.

Instead she felt tired and cleanly furious.

That was better than frightened.

In the kitchen, Haru said nothing.

Elira glanced through the open doorway.

He was standing with both palms resting around the cool teapot as if the fate of every star sat inside it.

She knew he wanted to ask whether she was all right.

She also knew he had learned enough not to make her answer before she chose the shape of it.

Elira folded the handwritten copy and placed it beside the outgoing letters.

Elira: "Krail, probably."

Haru shifted his weight in the doorway.

Elira: "No."

He stopped before turning fully.

Elira: "That was my answer."

For one long second, the room held both of them without tilting toward either side. Then Haru nodded.

Haru: "Will you show me when you want to?"

Elira's anger loosened by one thread.

Elira: "When I want to."

Her hand settled flat against the edge of the writing desk.

She stood, slower than she wanted, and returned to the door.

The Iven letter was gone. The Council form was gone. The copy remained, proof that a living hand had answered without asking anyone to carry the pen:

**I was not carried through that part. I walked.**

---

Afterward, Elira stood by the door with her hand against the wood.

Elira: "Cael should be here."

There were many wrong answers.

The world had taught me most of them.

He is in the record. He chose. He saved you. He is honored. All true. All insufficient.

Haru: "Yes."

I kept my hands still at my sides so she would not have to brace against a rescue.

Her hand curled into a fist.

Elira: "I am glad I am alive."

Haru: "Yes."

I let the truth stand without softening it.

Elira: "And I hate that his death is in the room whenever I say it."

The old cold behind my ribs answered.

This time I did not let it become a solution. I stood beside her.

Haru: "Then we make room for both."

Elira's eyes closed.

Elira: "Both again."

Haru: "Official practice."

She laughed once through the ache.

Elira: "The feather was unimpressive."

Haru: "It served the lesson."

Elira leaned her forehead against the door. I waited.

Eventually she turned and rested against me instead.

I put my arms around her after she did, not before.

The house did not glow. The wards did not sing. No witness crystal recorded the moment, and for once, none needed to.

Evening came blue and quiet, paused only for a short five-minute check-in on the folding mirror before Rhea cleared us for sleep.

We ate soup by the window. Elira fell asleep halfway through a sentence and woke angry about it. I did not laugh. That was wise. I did warm the soup again. That was wiser.

After dinner, she asked me to braid her hair.

I had never braided anything in my life. She discovered this quickly.

Elira: "Haru."

Haru: "Yes?"

Elira: "Are you tying a knot?"

Haru: "No."

Elira: "That pause says yes."

I carefully freed the strand.

Elira sat on the rug between my knees, shoulders shaking with quiet laughter as I failed with scholarly dedication. The fire burned low. The lake reflected moonlight through the window. Her pendant rested against her chest, dark and watchful, but not cold.

When I finally made something that resembled a braid if judged kindly from a distance, Elira touched it.

Elira: "Terrible."

Haru: "I'll improve."

Elira leaned back against my knees.

Elira: "Good."

The softness in that word pulled the room close around us, warm and unguarded.

She tilted her head back to look at me.

Elira: "Kiss me?"

The question was gentle.

It still made the Black Circle go silent. I bent down slowly.

Our first kiss beneath the silver-leaf tree had been quiet and almost impossible, full of the frightening joy of being chosen without being claimed. This one carried no veil, no vow spoken in shock, and no hidden rank between us.

Just Elira choosing, after death had touched her and politics had named her evidence, to ask for tenderness in a room by a lake. I kissed her softly.

She reached up and held my face with both hands. The braid fell apart. Neither of us cared.

Later, when we lay beside each other under the same blanket, Elira's head rested against my shoulder.

Elira: "Today felt almost normal."

Haru: "Parts of it."

Elira: "I liked the parts."

Haru: "So did I."

The lake moved outside.

The world waited beyond the trees with hearings, memoranda, Noctis fractures, and questions no one had earned the right to ask.

But inside the quiet place, Elira's breathing evened.

This time I slept too.

---

The third day began with Aira calling at breakfast and ruining the word immediately.

The folding check-in mirror beside the jam jar brightened while Elira was spreading pear jam with the careful seriousness of a person committing family treason.

Aira's face appeared upside down.

Aira: "Day three checkpoint! Wait-good morning, medically sanctioned honeymoon."

Elira choked.

I spilled tea on my sleeve.

Leon groaned somewhere behind Aira's shoulder.

Leon: "You promised not to open with that."

Aira rotated the mirror image upright.

Aira: "I promised to consider not opening with that."

Rhea's voice cut in from out of frame.

President Valmont: "This is an official welfare check."

Cassian: "With honeymoon oversight."

President Valmont: "Veyr."

Cassian: "Withdrawn."

Elira covered her face with one hand.

Elira: "I regret having friends."

Aira: "No, you don't. You regret that your friends are accurate."

I recovered the cup before it dripped onto the floor.

Haru: "It is recovery leave."

Aira looked directly at me through the mirror.

Aira: "Haru, you are alone with your official girlfriend in a lake house, under orders to rest, eat, sleep near each other, and stop treating romance like an emergency drill. I am not saying the Council invented a honeymoon. I am saying bureaucracy tripped and fell into one."

Elira's ears turned pink. The sight did something reckless to my pulse.

Professor Valen appeared beside Rhea, holding a file.

Professor Valen: "Aira's terminology is not medically recognized."

Aira: "Emotionally recognized."

Professor Valen: "Unfortunately."

Rhea cleared her throat.

President Valmont: "Actual update. Noctis filed two objections to the recovery order. Both were rejected. Senna Voss asked to delay Elira's medical testimony until Maelin clears it. High Councilor Krail is trying to frame staying close as unhealthy dependency."

Elira lowered her hand. The blush faded.

Haru: "Of course he is."

Rhea's gaze shifted to Elira.

President Valmont: "Your corrected welfare form reached my office before his summary did."

Aira leaned into view.

Aira: "For the record, 'Alive. Irritated.' has entered my permanent vocabulary."

Elira's chin lifted by a fraction.

Elira: "It was medically accurate."

Professor Valen: "It was politically smart because it exposed the trap."

President Valmont: "Exactly. Krail now has to argue against your conditions instead of pretending he only asked neutral questions."

I looked at Elira.

She did not look at me first.

She looked at the dimmed mirror edge, where her own reflection sat beside the Council seal without being absorbed by it. Good.

President Valmont: "He will get nowhere if you give him no public trouble today."

Aira: "Translation: please do not darken the sky unless someone earns it."

Haru: "I will try."

Leon leaned into view.

Leon: "Also, the water charm is holding?"

Elira smiled.

Elira: "Yes. Thank you."

Leon nodded too quickly and stepped back out of frame.

Cassian: "He practiced asking that normally."

Leon: "I did not."

Aira: "He did."

The mirror call ended with Rhea ordering us to answer the evening check-in and Aira loudly advising us to "do something emotionally irresponsible but medically moderate."

For a few seconds after the mirror dimmed, neither of us spoke.

Then Elira set down the jam knife.

Elira: "I want to go into town."

Every security map in my head unfolded at once. Elira watched it happen.

Elira: "Small rebellion."

Haru: "The town is outside the perimeter."

Elira: "The first market street is inside the outer ward Professor Valen inspected."

Haru: "There will be people."

Elira: "That is usually what towns contain."

I looked at the window.

Lake Velis village sat half a mile down the road, a cluster of slate roofs, fishing boats, and shop awnings bright against the shore. Ordinary people lived there. Ordinary people now knew the Black Circle was not a myth, because the whole world knew. Ordinary people would look. At me. At her.

At the girl who had died and returned.

At the boy who had nearly become an ending.

Elira reached across the table and touched my wrist.

Elira: "I do not want our first days away from Aurelis to teach us that safety means hiding from every face."

I knew she was right.

I hated that she was right while still weak enough that climbing the porch steps cost her breath.

Haru: "If you get tired, we leave."

Elira: "Agreed."

Haru: "If the crowd presses, we leave."

Elira: "I promise."

Haru: "If any relay-"

Elira squeezed my wrist.

Elira: "Haru."

I stopped. She smiled.

Elira: "Ask me what I want to buy."

The absurdity of the question took the edge off my warning before I could argue.

Haru: "What do you want to buy?"

Elira: "A ribbon."

Haru: "For your hair?"

Elira looked toward the bedroom, where my failed braid from the night before had been mercifully undone.

Elira: "For your continued education."

The decision to go into town took forty minutes to become an actual coat.

That was mostly my fault.

Elira sat on the edge of the bed while I arranged possible outer layers on the chair with the seriousness of a battle plan. Pale shawl. Dark shawl. Heavier cloak. Lighter cloak. The blue ribbon from Aira's packet. A small healing charm Maelin had labeled **ONLY IF DIZZY, NOT IF DRAMATIC**.

Elira watched me for almost a full minute.

Elira: "Haru."

Haru: "Yes?"

Elira: "You are choosing fabric like it will negotiate with assassins."

I looked at the cloaks.

Haru: "Some fabrics hide ward seams better."

Elira's mouth twitched.

Elira: "That was not a denial."

Haru: "No."

She reached for the pale shawl.

I handed it to her before remembering that handing it too quickly was also a kind of hovering. My arm stopped halfway.

Elira stared at the shawl suspended between us.

Elira: "Are we having a crisis about fabric?"

Haru: "Possibly."

Elira took it from me.

Elira: "I choose this one."

Haru: "Because it is lighter?"

Elira wrapped it around her shoulders.

Elira: "Because I like it."

The answer beat six security worries at once. I admired it. Reluctantly.

She pinned her hair back loosely with the blue ribbon, leaving a few strands free around her face to catch the morning light. She looked less like the Yellow Circle prodigy the world had watched die and more like a girl leaving a house on an ordinary errand.

Then she saw herself in the small mirror.

Her hand went to the pendant, and the air between us sobered.

Elira: "It shows."

Haru: "The pendant?"

Elira: "The fear."

I stepped closer, then stopped where she could see the choice.

Haru: "What do you want people to see?"

She looked at her reflection for a long time.

Elira: "Not that I am untouched."

Her voice stayed steady, hard-earned.

Elira: "I do not want them thinking I am grateful enough to behave, or that dying made me softer and easier to turn into a symbol."

Her fingers lowered from the pendant.

Elira: "I want them to see I am here. And that I chose the ribbon myself."

Haru: "Then that is what we carry."

She turned.

Elira: "Together?"

Haru: "Together."

The restoration house warmed beneath our feet. A second black ribbon edged in silver slipped from the desk drawer and landed on the floor between us. Elira looked down.

Elira: "Opinionated house."

Haru: "Interfering house."

The old silver in the floor did not react, which I chose to interpret as guilt.

Elira picked up the ribbon.

Elira: "We will buy one anyway."

Haru: "To avoid encouraging it?"

Elira: "To choose twice."

So we left: Elira in her pale shawl and blue ribbon, the dark pendant visible at her throat because hiding it would have given fear too much room; me in a dark coat with a calm I did not expect anyone who knew me to believe; the house's spare ribbon tucked in Elira's pocket like a small argument waiting for later.

The road to Lake Velis village ran between cedar trees and low stone walls. Wildflowers grew in gaps where frost had cracked the old mortar. Fishing nets hung from posts near the shore, drying in the wind. A boy about Leon's age repaired a boat rope and pretended not to stare until Elira waved.

He nearly dropped the rope. Elira smiled.

Elira: "Too much?"

Haru: "For him?"

Elira: "For me."

I considered lying. She deserved better.

Haru: "Some."

Elira gave a single, brief nod.

Elira: "Do not ask if we should go back."

Haru: "I was arranging the words."

Elira: "Unarrange them."

I kept them to myself.

At the outer ward marker, a thin line of silver crossed the road. It did not flare for rank. It did not test my Circle. It only warmed as Elira stepped over it, then again as I followed.

**VOLUNTARY EXIT.**

The impression settled into my mind like a hand closing gently around a record. Elira paused.

Elira: "It records leaving?"

Haru: "Voluntary."

She breathed out.

Elira: "Good."

Then, with a small defiance I loved before I understood it, she stepped backward over the line and forward again. The ward warmed twice.

**VOLUNTARY RETURN. VOLUNTARY EXIT.**

Elira's smile sharpened.

Elira: "I like that."

Haru: "The ward?"

Elira: "The correction."

She stepped into the village road. I followed, feeling the old house behind us accept that protection could include departure.

The village did look.

There was no avoiding that.

People paused with baskets in hand. A child tugged at her mother's sleeve. An old fisherman removed his cap when Elira passed, then seemed embarrassed by the fuss and put it back on badly. Two shopkeepers whispered my name without meaning for me to hear. Black Circle.

The words followed at a distance, no longer myth or secret and still far from understood.

Elira's hand tightened around mine.

I almost apologized for the attention.

Then I realized she was holding me steady too.

A ribbon seller near the fountain bowed so deeply that Elira's face changed.

Elira: "Please don't."

The woman straightened at once.

Ribbon Seller: "Sorry, Lady Vale."

Elira: "Elira is fine."

The woman's eyes flicked to me, then back to her.

Ribbon Seller: "Elira, then."

That small correction did more than the bow. Elira breathed easier.

She chose a blue ribbon first, then a gold one, then after a moment a narrow black ribbon edged in silver thread.

The seller hesitated before touching it.

I felt the market notice. Elira noticed too.

She picked up the black ribbon herself and held it against my sleeve.

Elira: "This one."

My heart did something undisciplined.

Haru: "For your hair?"

Elira: "For yours."

I stared at her. She looked entirely serious.

Haru: "My hair is not long enough for a ribbon."

Elira: "Then I will improvise badly and you will be gracious."

The ribbon seller made a small sound that might have been a laugh before fear caught it. Elira smiled at her.

Elira: "He is very gracious under ribbon-based adversity."

The seller relaxed enough to wrap the ribbons with ordinary care.

As we left, the child who had been staring from beside the fountain stepped forward.

Child: "Are you the Black Circle?"

Her mother went pale.

Mother: "Lysa."

I crouched before panic could spread.

That made several people tense.

So I kept my hands visible.

Haru: "My name is Haru."

The child considered this.

Lysa: "But are you?"

Elira's hand rested on my shoulder, steady and unhurried.

Haru: "Yes."

I kept my eyes level with hers without hiding behind a softer rank.

The word entered the market like a stone into water. No disguise. No old Green lie to hide behind.

Lysa frowned.

Lysa: "You don't look like the scary drawings."

Aira would have loved her.

Haru: "That is probably good."

Lysa nodded.

Lysa: "My brother says Black Circle means you can break mountains."

Haru: "Breaking mountains causes problems for people who live near mountains."

The child thought that over with grave respect.

Lysa: "So you don't?"

Haru: "I try not to break things that do not need breaking."

Elira's fingers moved once against my shoulder.

The mother bowed her head, not deeply this time.

Mother: "Thank you."

I did not know for which part. Maybe neither did she.

The market did not return to normal after that. It tried.

That made it kinder than a council chamber.

The ribbon seller began wrapping the black ribbon again because her hands needed something to do. The old fisherman bought apples he clearly did not need. Lysa's mother took her daughter's shoulders and whispered something too soft for ordinary hearing, so I made myself not listen with anything beyond it. Elira noticed.

Elira: "Thank you."

Haru: "For what?"

Elira: "Not hearing everything just because you can."

The compliment entered a place in me I had not known needed it.

Haru: "I am learning."

Elira's smile was tired and proud.

Then a man near the baker's stall bowed shallowly, with the stiff care of someone who did not know what else to do.

Man: "Lady Vale. Aerlen."

He said my name like a stone he was not sure he was allowed to hold. Elira turned toward him.

Elira: "Good morning."

He swallowed.

Man: "My daughter is Green Circle. She was at the academy gate two days ago."

Mira's sign flashed in my memory.

**RECOVERY IS NOT ABSENCE**

The man looked at me, then immediately away.

Man: "She said you raised your hand to the Noctis students too."

Elira's expression softened.

Elira: "I did."

Man: "She cried about it."

He looked mortified to have said that aloud.

Elira did not save him from the feeling by pretending it was nothing.

Elira: "I am glad she saw them."

The man's eyes filled. He bowed again, smaller.

Man: "Thank you."

I only caught the edges of what that gratitude meant to him, and left the rest undisturbed.

We bought bread from his stall because leaving without doing so would have made the conversation too solemn. Elira chose two rolls and one small pastry shaped like a crescent moon. The baker added a second pastry without charging. I opened my mouth.

Elira stepped lightly on my foot, just enough to stop me.

Haru: "Thank you."

The baker looked relieved by the ordinary words.

Elira waited until we were three stalls away.

Elira: "You were about to argue about pastry."

Haru: "Unpaid goods create obligation."

Elira: "Sometimes they create breakfast."

Haru: "It is almost noon."

Elira: "Then emergency breakfast."

She tore one pastry in half and offered me the larger piece. I looked at it.

Haru: "Hierarchy matters?"

Elira: "Aira has infected us both."

We ate pastry beside the village fountain.

The fountain was small and practical, nothing like Aurelis' repaired courtyard fountain or the Wounded City markers. Water spilled from a stone fish into a round basin where children had thrown copper coins. No hidden black ring. No public relay. No old system waiting to wake under pressure. Just water.

Elira watched it with such focus that I worried until she spoke.

Elira: "I used to want a fountain in the Vale winter garden."

Haru: "Why?"

Elira: "Because I thought the academy fountains were beautiful when I first visited Aurelis. I was nine. Everything gold looked like a promise then."

Her mouth curved without quite smiling.

Elira: "My mother said indoor fountains were impractical. My father said impractical things were useful if they made a house kinder. They compromised on a birdbath."

Haru: "Did birds use it?"

Elira: "One extremely arrogant sparrow."

Haru: "A successful compromise."

She laughed.

The sound moved through the market differently than the word Black Circle had.

People heard it and tried not to stare. Some failed. Elira let them fail.

Then the fountain water rippled.

My hand moved before thought, reaching for her instead of a ward. She caught my fingers.

The ripple had been a coin dropping from Lysa's hand. The child froze.

So did half the square.

My Black Circle stayed quiet. My face, less so. Elira squeezed my hand.

Haru: "Sorry."

Lysa looked at me with blunt horror.

Lysa: "Did I almost make you break a mountain?"

The square's false wind dropped away.

Elira pressed her lips together.

I could feel the laugh in her hand before I heard it.

Haru: "No."

Lysa: "Oh."

Haru: "Maybe a cup."

Elira turned her face away. Her shoulders shook.

The mother looked as if she had aged several years and then been handed them back. Lysa considered the answer.

Lysa: "Cups are replaceable."

Haru: "That is what I have heard."

The square exhaled in ragged pieces. The baker laughed first. The ribbon seller followed.

Then the old fisherman, who had bought apples for no reason, chimed in.

Old Fisherman: "Depends on the cup."

That broke the rest of the tension cleanly.

The market resumed around us, not normal, not careless, but less terrified of the fact that I had answered a child and survived being known. Elira leaned closer.

Elira: "You made a joke."

Haru: "A small one."

Elira: "Publicly."

Haru: "Under pressure."

Elira: "Aira will document this as growth."

Haru: "Please do not tell her."

Elira's smile turned dangerous.

Elira: "I am absolutely telling her."

We walked one more row of stalls, stopped by a harbor porch for warm cider and dried pears, and lingered through the long afternoon among the net-menders' benches because I wanted to prove to myself that leaving immediately after a flinch was not the only kind of safety. As shadows lengthened, she chose a small packet of tea for Maelin, a wooden bookmark for Professor Valen, and a dark blue thread spool for no reason she would admit.

At the edge of the market, a notice crystal flickered in the window of the post office against the slanting late sun. My name appeared. Not fully.

Only in the headline passing through the public relay:

**COUNCIL MINORITY QUESTIONS BLACK CIRCLE PROXIMITY DURING RECOVERY LEAVE**

Elira saw it before I could step between her and the glass. Her expression closed.

The day lost some of its warmth.

Haru: "We can go."

Elira stared at the notice until the words cycled away.

Elira: "No."

Haru: "Elira."

Elira: "I am not going to let Krail become the last thing I saw in town."

She turned deliberately to the flower stall next door.

A woman there was arranging white lake flowers like the ones Professor Valen had left in the restoration house. Elira bought three stems and held them in both hands.

Elira: "There."

Haru: "There?"

Elira looked back at the post office window, where the headline had returned.

Elira: "Now he is beside flowers."

She had not erased Krail's headline. She had simply refused to let it keep the whole window.

I carried the parcels so her hands could keep the stems.

## The Fish Charm

The last stall before the road back to the house belonged to a woodcarver who had packed everything except one small fish.

It hung from a blue cord near the corner of the awning, one fin shorter than the other and a shallow knife mark crossing its painted scales. No magic moved inside it. No ward answered when I touched the cord. Only wood shaped by a patient hand that had slipped once and kept going.

Behind us, the post office window still caught the low afternoon sun, Krail's headline cycling quietly behind the glass.

The carver noticed me looking.

Woodcarver: "Travel charm. Lake families give them to people who need help remembering the way home."

Elira shifted the flowers to her other arm so she could see it properly.

Elira: "You stopped walking for it."

Haru: "I noticed it."

Elira: "Those are different sentences."

They were. Before Aurelis, I would have chosen the safer one and kept moving. Before Krail started writing separation into polite, neutral-looking forms, I might not have felt the sudden, quiet need to own a compass made of wood and string.

I bought the fish.

The carver accepted my coin without bowing, thanking the Black Circle, or asking whether mountains were safe. She shortened the cord because I asked. The exchange lasted less than a minute and changed no law in Aurelis, yet my thumb stayed over the small notch in its wooden fin as if memorizing a landmark.

On the path home, Elira hooked one finger through the blue cord where it emerged from my closed hand.

Elira: "Where will you keep it?"

I looked toward the restoration house, its warm lamps already lit between the cedars while the ridge beyond the lake darkened toward evening.

Haru: "Somewhere I can find it if someone tries to lose the road."

Elira's fingers tightened gently around the cord before letting it go.

On the walk back, she grew tired before she admitted it.

I noticed the change in her steps. The way her hand became heavier in mine. The way her smile stayed in place by discipline instead of ease.

Haru: "We stop for a minute."

Elira sighed.

Elira: "You are correct."

Haru: "You sound offended."

Elira: "I am offended that my body agrees with you."

We took the lake path rather than the road. Halfway home, she stopped beneath cedar shade and leaned against me with trust instead of collapse.

I held her with one arm around her shoulders.

Elira: "The child asked you directly."

Haru: "Yes."

The water beyond the reeds stayed flat and gray under the cooling sky.

Elira: "You answered."

Haru: "It is public now."

Elira: "That is not the same as being honest without armor."

The cedar branches moved above us.

I looked at the path ahead, then down at her.

Haru: "I was afraid."

Elira: "I know."

Haru: "Not of her."

Elira: "I know that too."

Haru: "Of how much easier it was when no one knew enough to ask."

Elira leaned her forehead against my shoulder.

Elira: "Secrets can be lonely even when they protect you."

I thought of the Moonlit Archive. Her face lit by black and silver. Her hand reaching for mine when anyone else would have stepped back.

Haru: "You made mine less lonely."

She looked up.

Elira: "Then let me keep doing it."

We stood there until her strength returned.
